Introduction: How to Read a Symbol

A symbol is a picture that does more work than a picture should be able to do. A drawing of a dog is just a dog. But a drawing of an eye inside a triangle, surrounded by rays, sets off a whole chain of thoughts in the person who sees it. One person thinks of church. Another thinks of the dollar bill. Another thinks of the Freemasons. Another thinks of secret societies, or of ancient Egypt, or of a television show they once watched about conspiracies. The image is the same. What it means depends on what the viewer brings to it.

This is the first lesson of reading symbols, and it is the most important one: a symbol does not have a single fixed meaning that lives inside the image itself. Its meaning comes from use. People give symbols meaning by how they use them, again and again, over years and centuries. When the same image is used by many different groups, it gathers layers of meaning like sediment at the bottom of a river. To read a symbol well, you have to be willing to dig through those layers carefully, without assuming that the top layer is the only one, and without assuming that the deepest layer is automatically the true one.

Three questions

Throughout this book, when we look at a symbol, we will ask three questions.

The first question is: where did it come from? This is the historical question. We want to know when an image first appeared, who made it, and what it seems to have meant to them. Often the honest answer is that we do not know exactly. Ancient people did not always write down why they carved what they carved. Where the evidence is thin, this book will say so plainly rather than filling the gap with guesses dressed up as facts.

The second question is: how has it traveled? Symbols move. They are borrowed, adapted, and reinterpreted. The eye that watches over a Renaissance painting of the Trinity is not the same as the eye painted on the prow of a Mediterranean fishing boat, even though both are eyes. The pyramid on the Great Seal of the United States is not a copy of the pyramids of Giza, even though it was clearly inspired by them. Following a symbol through time shows us how people in different places solved the same problem: how to show, in a single image, something that cannot be seen.

The third question is: what does it mean here? This is the question that matters most for this book. The Conscientia emblem of Meechie's World Inc borrows from many traditions, but it is its own thing. It was made for a purpose, at a particular time, by a particular person. When we ask what the eye means in our emblem, the answer is not found in Egypt or in Philadelphia. It is found in the work of the company and in the promises written around the emblem itself.

Seeing the invisible

Why do people make symbols at all? One answer is that symbols let us point at things that have no shape. Justice has no shape. Conscience has no shape. Wisdom, providence, truth, memory: none of these can be photographed. Yet people need to talk about them, to rally around them, to remind each other of them. So we borrow shapes from the visible world and ask them to stand in for the invisible one.

The eye is perhaps the most natural choice of all. We know from our own experience that seeing is knowing. When we say "I see," we often mean "I understand." When we want to say that something is watched over, protected, or judged, we picture an eye. When we want to say that something cannot be hidden, we picture an eye that never closes. It is no accident that this image appears independently in so many cultures. It speaks to something basic in human experience: the feeling of being seen, and the hope, or the fear, that our actions are known.

The pyramid and the book work the same way. The pyramid is the most stable shape there is. It is wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, so it does not fall over. It points upward. It was, for thousands of years, the tallest thing human beings had ever built. It is a natural picture of permanence, of order, and of aspiration. The book is the natural picture of knowledge that lasts beyond a single life. A spoken word disappears; a written word remains. An open book invites reading. It says: the knowledge here is not locked away.

Symbols and fear

It would be dishonest to write a book about the all-seeing eye without addressing the fear that has gathered around it. In the last few decades, the eye in the triangle has become, for many people, a sign of hidden power. It is said to be the mark of the Illuminati, of a secret group that controls governments and banks and entertainment. Musicians are accused of flashing it. Logos are examined for hidden triangles. A whole industry of videos and books exists to find the eye everywhere and to treat each sighting as proof of a conspiracy.

This book takes those fears seriously enough to examine them. Chapter Seven looks at where the Illuminati story came from, what the historical Illuminati actually was, and why the eye became attached to it. The short version is that the historical group was real, small, and short-lived, and that it did not create the eye symbol, did not design the Great Seal, and did not survive the eighteenth century in any organized form. The longer version is more interesting, and it tells us a great deal about how symbols gain and lose their power.

For now, it is enough to say that a symbol is not responsible for every use people make of it. A cross can mark a hospital or a battlefield. A flag can be raised in celebration or in hate. The eye has been used by priests, painters, patriots, and pranksters. In the Conscientia emblem, it is used for one reason: to remind us that we work in the open, and that conscience watches.

Chapter One

The First Eye

The eye is the lamp of the body.
Matthew 6:22

Before there were words for it, there was the experience of being looked at. Every human being knows it. A newborn baby, only days old, will turn toward a face and fix on the eyes. Long before an infant understands language, it understands that eyes matter: that the eyes of another person carry attention, recognition, warmth, or warning. Scientists who study infants have found that babies prefer to look at faces with open eyes rather than closed ones, and that they follow the direction of another person's gaze within the first year of life. We are, from the very beginning, creatures who watch watchers.

This simple fact sits at the root of every eye symbol in this book. When an ancient Egyptian painted an eye on a coffin, when a medieval artist placed an eye inside a triangle, when the designers of an American seal set an eye above a pyramid, they were all drawing on the same deep instinct. An eye is not just a part of the body. It is the sign of a mind behind it. To see an eye is to know that someone is there.

The power of the gaze

Researchers in psychology have run many experiments on what happens when people feel watched. One of the best known took place in a university break room in England in the early 2000s. Staff paid for their coffee and tea through an honesty box. Above the box, the researchers posted a small picture that changed every week. Some weeks it showed flowers. Other weeks it showed a pair of eyes. In the weeks when the eyes were posted, people paid noticeably more for their drinks. Nobody was actually watching. It was only a picture. But the picture of eyes was enough to make people behave a little more honestly.

Later studies have argued about how strong this effect really is, and some have failed to repeat it. Science is like that; one experiment is never the last word. But the basic idea behind the study is ancient and widely shared: when we believe we are seen, we act differently. We remember our obligations. We think about our reputation. We become, in a word, more conscientious.

That word will come back again and again in this book, because it is the word written beneath the eye in the emblem of Meechie's World Inc. Conscientia, in Latin, is the root of our word conscience. The connection between the watching eye and the inner voice of conscience is one of the oldest ideas in human thought. The eye outside us becomes, over time, an eye inside us. We learn to watch ourselves.

Eyes in the earliest art

When did people first begin to draw eyes? The honest answer is that we cannot know for certain. The oldest surviving art, painted and carved tens of thousands of years ago in caves and rock shelters, is full of animals: horses, bison, deer, mammoths, lions. Human figures are rarer, and faces rarer still. But eyes do appear, sometimes as part of animals, sometimes as simple circles or dots that may or may not be eyes.

What we can say is that, once people began to settle in villages and build lasting monuments, eyes appear more and more often. In the ancient Near East, archaeologists have found large numbers of small carved figures with exaggerated eyes. At a site in northern Syria called Tell Brak, excavators uncovered hundreds of small stone figurines from around 3500 to 3300 BCE that are little more than a pair of huge carved eyes on top of a flat body. Archaeologists call them "eye idols," and the building where many were found is known as the Eye Temple. No one knows exactly what these figures meant to the people who made them. They may have been offerings left at a shrine, images of worshippers standing forever before their god, or charms of protection. But their message is unmistakable even across five thousand years: the eye is the point.

In the cities of Sumer, in what is now southern Iraq, worshippers set up statues of themselves in temples, standing with their hands clasped and their eyes wide open, inlaid with shell and dark stone. A famous group of these statues was found at Tell Asmar, the ancient city of Eshnunna. The figures stare upward with enormous round eyes. The idea seems to have been that the statue would stand in the presence of the god on the worshipper's behalf, always attentive, always awake. The open eye was a sign of devotion. It meant: I am here, and I am paying attention.

The eye that protects

Alongside the eye that worships, there is the eye that protects. Across much of the world, people have long believed that a harmful glance could bring bad luck, illness, or misfortune. This is the belief known as the evil eye. It appears in ancient Greek and Roman writing, in Jewish and Islamic tradition, in South Asia, in Latin America, and across the Mediterranean. The idea is that envy, carried by a look, can do real damage. A person who stares too long at a healthy child, a fine horse, or a prosperous house might, without even meaning to, cause it harm.

The response to the evil eye has very often been another eye. In Turkey and Greece, one of the most familiar sights is the nazar, a disk of blue glass with concentric circles of white and darker blue, so that it looks like a staring eye. It hangs in homes, cars, and shops, and is pinned to the clothing of babies. The logic is simple: the protective eye looks back at the harmful one and turns it away. In North Africa and the Middle East, the hamsa, a hand-shaped charm, often has an eye in its palm. Fishermen in Malta, Portugal, and other Mediterranean lands have painted eyes on the bows of their boats for generations, so that the boat can see its way and be protected on the water.

These protective eyes remind us that the watching eye is not always a figure of judgment or fear. Very often it is a figure of care. A parent watches over a child. A guard watches over a city. A lighthouse keeper watches over the sea. To be watched over is to be looked after.

The eye as the window

There is another ancient idea about eyes that is worth noticing. Many traditions have thought of the eyes as a window, both outward and inward. The eyes let light into the body, and in some way they also let the soul show through. Ancient Greek thinkers argued about how vision worked. Some, following the philosopher Empedocles and later Plato, believed that the eye sent out a kind of fire or ray that touched the objects it saw. Others, like the atomists, thought that thin films or images came off objects and entered the eye. It was not until the work of the Arab scholar Ibn al-Haytham, writing in Cairo around the year 1000, that a clear and testable account of vision as light entering the eye was laid out. His great Book of Optics changed how scholars across the Islamic world and later in Europe understood sight.

Whether the eye sends light out or takes light in, the important thing for our story is that the eye was always connected with light. To see, there must be light. In darkness, the eye is useless. This pairing of the eye with light, and of blindness with darkness, runs through almost every tradition that uses the eye as a symbol. It is why the eye in the emblem of Meechie's World Inc is surrounded by rays, and why the motto beneath it speaks of light out of darkness.

In Christian scripture, Jesus says that the eye is the lamp of the body, and that if the eye is healthy, the whole body will be full of light. The saying is about more than physical sight. It is about how we look at the world, whether with generosity or with envy, with clarity or with confusion. A clear eye lights up a whole life.

Seeing and knowing

In English, as in many languages, the vocabulary of seeing is bound up with the vocabulary of knowing. We say "I see" when we mean "I understand." We speak of insight, foresight, and hindsight. We call a wise person a seer or a visionary. We say that the truth has come to light, that someone has an enlightened mind, that a plan is clear. A witness is someone who has seen. Evidence comes from a Latin word meaning that which is seen clearly. The word idea comes from a Greek root connected to seeing. Even the word wisdom is related, through old Germanic roots, to the same family of words that gave us vision and video.

This is not an accident of language. For human beings, sight is the strongest of the senses, the one through which we gather the most information about the world. It is natural that we would use the language of sight to talk about knowledge of every kind. And it is natural that, when people wanted to picture a being or a power that knows everything, they pictured an eye that sees everything.

The eye that never sleeps

Human eyes close. We blink thousands of times a day, and we sleep for a third of our lives. A watcher who never closes his eyes is therefore something more than human. In the ancient world, the gods were often described as all-seeing. In Greek tradition, Helios, the sun, saw everything that happened on earth during the day, and so he was called on as a witness to oaths. In Hindu tradition, the sun god Surya is sometimes called the eye of the gods. In the Hebrew scriptures, the psalmist says that the one who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. The image of the unsleeping eye became a way of talking about a protection that never fails and a justice that never misses anything.

The Greek myth of Argus Panoptes, the giant with a hundred eyes, captures the same idea in a more playful form. Argus was set by the goddess Hera to guard a young woman named Io, and because he had so many eyes, some of them were always awake. Even when he slept, some eyes stayed open. The god Hermes finally defeated him by lulling all his eyes to sleep with music and stories. After Argus died, the story goes, Hera placed his eyes in the tail of the peacock, which is why the peacock's feathers are covered with eye-shaped spots. His name, Panoptes, means "all-seeing," and it survives in the English word panoptic.

From many eyes to one

As we will see in the chapters that follow, there was a long movement in many traditions from many eyes to one. The hundred eyes of Argus, the many eyes of the evil-eye charm, the pairs of eyes on the boats and statues, gradually give way to a single eye, alone, often set within a shape: a circle, a triangle, a cloud, a burst of light. The single eye is more abstract. It no longer belongs to any particular body. It stands for pure attention, pure awareness, pure witness.

That single eye is the one we find in the Conscientia emblem. It does not belong to a person. It does not belong to a god in any particular religion. It belongs to the idea of conscience itself: the awareness that watches over our work, that keeps us honest when no one else is looking, and that sees clearly through the darkness.

What the first eye teaches

Before moving on to Egypt and the most famous eye of the ancient world, it is worth pausing to gather what this first chapter has shown.

The eye is one of the oldest and most widespread symbols in human history. It appears in places and cultures that had no contact with one another, which suggests that it springs from something basic in human nature: our sensitivity to being seen.

The eye has carried several different meanings, often at the same time. It is the eye of devotion, which stays open before the divine. It is the eye of protection, which turns away harm. It is the eye of knowledge, which sees and therefore understands. It is the eye of witness, which cannot be deceived. And it is the eye of judgment, which sees what we do and holds us to account.

The eye is bound up with light. Wherever eye symbols appear, light is rarely far away: in rays, in suns, in lamps, in fire.

And finally, the outer eye tends to become an inner one. The watching eye on the wall becomes, over time, the watching eye of conscience. This is the journey the Conscientia emblem asks us to remember. The eye is not out there, spying on us. It is in here, reminding us who we are.

With that in mind, let us turn to the land where the eye became one of the most powerful images ever made: ancient Egypt.

Chapter Two

Egypt: The Eye of Horus and the Eye of Ra

What was broken is made whole.
the meaning of the wedjat eye

If you ask most people to name an ancient eye symbol, they will name the Eye of Horus. With its bold outline, its painted brow, and the curling lines that fall from beneath it, it is one of the most recognizable images from the ancient world. It appears on jewelry, tattoos, album covers, and shop signs. It is printed on T-shirts in tourist markets in Cairo and on the walls of tattoo parlors in Pittsburgh. Yet for all its fame, the Eye of Horus is often misunderstood, and it is frequently confused with a second Egyptian eye, the Eye of Ra. This chapter untangles the two and explains why the Egyptian eye matters to anyone who wants to understand the eye in the Conscientia emblem.

A civilization of symbols

Ancient Egyptian civilization lasted for roughly three thousand years, from the unification of the country around 3100 BCE until it came under Roman rule in 30 BCE. Over that immense span of time, the Egyptians developed one of the richest systems of symbolic images the world has ever known. Their writing, which the Greeks later called hieroglyphs, meaning sacred carvings, used pictures of real things, such as birds, reeds, water, eyes, and hands, to stand for sounds and ideas. Egyptian art and Egyptian writing were never fully separate. A painted scene on a tomb wall could be read, and a line of hieroglyphs could be admired as art.

In this world, the eye was everywhere. The hieroglyph of an eye could stand for the verb "to see" or for the act of doing or making. Painted eyes appeared on the sides of coffins, so that the person inside could look out at the world of the living and at the rising sun. Protective eye amulets were placed among the wrappings of mummies. Eyes were painted on boats and carved on temple walls. To understand the Eye of Horus, we have to begin with the god himself.

Horus, the falcon god

Horus was one of the most important gods in Egyptian religion. He was usually shown as a falcon or as a man with the head of a falcon. The falcon, flying high above the land and seeing everything below with its sharp eyes, was a natural image for a god of the sky and of kingship. From very early times the Egyptian king was identified with Horus. The living king was the Horus on earth, the protector of the land and the keeper of order.

In the most widely told version of his story, Horus was the son of the god Osiris and the goddess Isis. Osiris had been king of Egypt, but he was murdered by his jealous brother Set, the god of storms, deserts, and disorder. Isis gathered her husband's body and, through her magic, conceived a son, Horus, who grew up in hiding in the marshes of the Nile Delta. When he came of age, Horus challenged Set for the throne of his father. Their struggle was long and violent. The ancient texts describe a series of contests and battles, some of them strange and even comic to modern readers.

During one of these battles, Set attacked Horus and tore out or damaged his eye. In some versions the eye was ripped into pieces; in others it was swallowed or thrown away. The eye was then healed and restored. Different texts give the credit to different gods. In some, it is Thoth, the ibis-headed god of wisdom, writing, and the moon, who finds the pieces and makes the eye whole again. In others, it is the goddess Hathor who heals the eye with milk. Once restored, the eye was called the wedjat, or more fully the wedjat eye, a word usually translated as "the sound one" or "the whole one."

The meaning of wholeness

The name wedjat is the key to understanding the Eye of Horus. It is an eye that was injured and made whole. It is a symbol not just of seeing, but of healing, of restoration, and of the triumph of order over chaos. Set had tried to destroy it; the gods brought it back. It became one of the most popular protective symbols in all of Egyptian history.

According to the myth, Horus gave his restored eye as an offering to his dead father Osiris, and this gift helped to bring Osiris back to life in the afterworld, where he became the ruler and judge of the dead. Because of this, the Eye of Horus came to stand for offerings in general. In Egyptian funerary texts, offerings of food, drink, and incense are often called the Eye of Horus. To offer something to the gods or to the dead was, in a sense, to give the healed eye again, renewing life and order.

Wedjat amulets were made by the thousands. They were carved from stone, cast in metal, and molded in a glazed ceramic material called faience, which gave them a bright blue or green color. They were worn by the living and placed on the bodies of the dead. A wedjat amulet was meant to protect its wearer, to keep him or her whole, and to restore what had been damaged. Many survive today in museums around the world. Some are tiny, no bigger than a fingernail. Others are elaborate pieces of jewelry, combined with other symbols and set in gold.

The shape of the eye

The Eye of Horus has a distinctive shape. It is a human eye, outlined boldly as Egyptian artists painted the eyes of people and gods, with a heavy brow above it. Beneath the eye there are two markings: a line that falls straight down, sometimes ending in a small curl, and a long line that sweeps backward and curls into a spiral. These markings are thought to come from the facial markings of a falcon, specifically the dark stripes beneath the eyes of certain falcons, such as the lanner falcon or the peregrine. So the Eye of Horus is both a human eye and a falcon's eye at once, fitting for a god who was both man and bird.

The fractions question

You may have read that each part of the Eye of Horus represents a fraction: one half, one quarter, one eighth, one sixteenth, one thirty-second, and one sixty-fourth, adding up to sixty-three sixty-fourths. According to this account, the missing sixty-fourth is the piece that Thoth supplied by magic. This idea is very popular, and it has a real basis: some Egyptian texts do write certain fractions, used for measuring grain, with signs that look like parts of the eye.

But scholars today are cautious. The fraction signs and the parts of the eye do not match up as neatly as the popular story suggests, and some Egyptologists believe that the link between the eye and the fractions was made later, or that the resemblance between some of the signs is a coincidence that was later given a mythological explanation. The honest position is that there is a real connection between some measurement signs and the eye, but that the tidy story of the eye as a complete set of fractions is at best a simplification. It makes a lovely story about wholeness and the missing piece, and in that sense it fits the meaning of the wedjat well. But it should not be presented as settled fact.

The Eye of Ra

The second great Egyptian eye is the Eye of Ra. Ra was the sun god, the creator, the king of the gods, who sailed across the sky each day in a boat and through the underworld each night. The Eye of Ra is not simply the god's eye in the way that a human has eyes. It is a force, almost a being in its own right, that goes out from the sun god to act in the world. It is fierce and dangerous. It is usually thought of as female, and it is identified with several goddesses, including Hathor, Sekhmet, Bastet, Wadjet, and Mut.

One famous myth tells how Ra, growing old, learned that humans were plotting against him. He sent out his Eye in the form of the lion goddess Sekhmet to punish them. Sekhmet slaughtered so many people that Ra feared she would wipe out humanity altogether. To stop her, he had a great quantity of beer dyed red to look like blood and poured over the fields. Sekhmet drank it, became drunk, and fell asleep. When she awoke, her rage had passed, and she was transformed into the gentle Hathor. Humanity was saved.

The Eye of Ra is often shown as a cobra, the uraeus, rearing up on the brow of gods and kings, ready to spit fire at enemies. It is also closely linked to the sun disk itself. Where the Eye of Horus stands for healing and wholeness, the Eye of Ra stands for the protective and destructive power of the sun, a power that can be terrible but that keeps chaos at bay.

Left and right, moon and sun

Egyptian texts sometimes connect the two eyes of a sky god with the sun and the moon. In this way of thinking, the right eye of the sky god is the sun and the left eye is the moon. The Eye of Horus, the eye that was injured and restored, came to be linked especially with the moon, which wanes and waxes, seeming to be torn apart and then made whole again each month. Thoth, who restored the eye, was himself a moon god. The Eye of Ra, by contrast, was linked with the sun. In practice the Egyptians themselves did not always keep these ideas strictly separate. The two eyes overlap in many texts, and the same amulet could be understood in different ways by different people.

For our purposes, the important thing is to recognize that the Egyptians did not have one single eye symbol with one meaning. They had a family of eye symbols, with related but different meanings: healing, wholeness, offering, protection, solar power, divine anger, and the watching presence of the gods.

The eye and the pyramid

It is tempting to connect the Egyptian eye directly with the pyramid, since both are so closely associated with Egypt in the modern imagination. But the Egyptians themselves did not place the Eye of Horus at the top of their pyramids. The combination of an eye with a pyramid or triangle, as we see it on the American dollar bill or in the Conscientia emblem, is a much later idea, as later chapters will show.

What the Egyptians did place at the top of their pyramids was a capstone, called a pyramidion, often made of fine stone and sometimes covered in gold or electrum so that it would catch the first light of the sun. Some surviving pyramidia are carved with images of the sun god and with a pair of eyes looking out. The pyramidion of the pharaoh Amenemhat III, now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, is carved with a winged sun disk and a pair of wedjat eyes, gazing toward the rising sun. So there is a genuine ancient link between the pyramid's peak, the sun, and the eye, even if it does not take the form of the single eye in a floating capstone that we know today.

Why Egypt matters to the emblem

The eye in the Conscientia emblem is not the Eye of Horus and it is not the Eye of Ra. It is not drawn in the Egyptian style, and it does not belong to any Egyptian god. But it inherits something from both. From the Eye of Horus, it inherits the idea of wholeness restored, of something broken being made right again. That is exactly the work Meechie's World Inc tries to do for people whose legal paperwork, businesses, or creative careers have been damaged or neglected: to help put the pieces back together. From the Eye of Ra, it inherits the idea of a light that drives back chaos.

Above all, Egypt teaches us that the eye was never just a picture of an organ of the body. From the very beginning of recorded history, it was a picture of presence, of protection, and of power used to restore order. The Egyptians understood that symbols could do work in the world, that wearing a wedjat or carving it on a coffin was a way of calling its power into one's life. Modern people may not share their beliefs about magic, but we still understand the basic point. A symbol worn with intention reminds us of what we hope for and what we stand for.

A note on respect

Because the Eye of Horus is so popular, it is sometimes used carelessly, as if it were just a cool design with no history. It is worth remembering that it was a sacred symbol for millions of people over thousands of years. Using it, or anything inspired by it, should be done with a sense of that history. The Conscientia emblem does not copy the Egyptian eye, partly out of that respect. It takes its place in a long line of eye symbols without pretending to be something it is not.

In the next chapter, we will travel beyond Egypt to see how other ancient peoples, from India to Scandinavia, pictured the watching eye.

Key Ideas

  • Egypt had a family of eye symbols, not one: the Eye of Horus and the Eye of Ra mean different things.
  • The wedjat, the Eye of Horus, is the eye that was injured and made whole: a symbol of healing and restoration.
  • The popular story that the Eye of Horus is a complete set of fractions is a simplification that scholars treat with caution.

Questions for Reflection

  1. What in your life or community has been broken and could be made whole again?
  2. Why do you think people still wear the Eye of Horus thousands of years after Egyptian religion ended?
  3. How can we use symbols from other cultures with respect for their history?

Chapter Three

Eyes of the Ancient World

Wisdom is bought at a price.
a lesson of the Norse tale of Odin at Mimir's well

Egypt gave the world its most famous ancient eye, but it was far from the only civilization to make the eye a central symbol. From the river valleys of India to the fjords of Scandinavia, from the temples of Mesopotamia to the hills of Nepal, people pictured divine sight, inner vision, and the protective gaze in ways that still echo today. This chapter travels across the ancient world to gather these eyes together. None of them is the direct ancestor of the eye in the Conscientia emblem. But together they show how widely shared, and how deeply rooted, the idea of the watching eye really is.

Mesopotamia: the eyes before the gods

We have already met the eye idols of Tell Brak and the wide-eyed worshipper statues of Sumer. In the later civilizations of Mesopotamia, the Babylonians and Assyrians, the gods themselves were described as all-seeing. The sun god, called Utu by the Sumerians and Shamash by the Babylonians and Assyrians, crossed the sky each day and saw everything that happened beneath him. Because nothing escaped his sight, he was the god of justice. Wrongdoers might hide from human judges, but they could not hide from the sun.

The most famous image of Shamash appears at the top of the stone pillar on which the laws of King Hammurabi of Babylon were carved, around 1750 BCE. The pillar, now in the Louvre in Paris, shows the king standing respectfully before the seated sun god, who hands him the symbols of authority. Beneath this scene are the laws themselves, nearly three hundred of them, written in cuneiform script. The message of the carving is clear: the king's justice comes from the god who sees everything. Law is grounded in sight.

This connection between the all-seeing sun, law, and justice is worth holding on to. It will appear again and again in this book, and it lies at the heart of the Conscientia emblem, where the eye sits above an open book and the motto declares, We seek justice.

India: the third eye

In the religious traditions of India, the eye takes on a striking form: the third eye. The god Shiva, one of the principal deities of Hinduism, is often shown with a third eye in the middle of his forehead. With his two ordinary eyes he sees the physical world. With the third, he sees beyond it. In some stories the third eye is a weapon of terrible power. When the god of desire, Kama, disturbed Shiva's meditation by shooting him with an arrow of love, Shiva opened his third eye and a blast of fire burned Kama to ashes.

The third eye is also connected with the idea of inner vision and spiritual awakening. In many forms of Hindu and yogic thought, the point between the eyebrows is the site of the ajna chakra, one of the energy centers of the subtle body. It is associated with intuition, insight, and the perception of truth beyond the senses. Many Hindus wear a mark, the tilaka or bindi, on this spot, for reasons that vary by tradition, region, and personal meaning, including devotion, blessing, and cultural identity.

The idea of a third eye has traveled far beyond India. In modern popular culture, the phrase "third eye" is often used loosely for intuition or spiritual insight. Some writers have linked it to the pineal gland, a small structure deep in the brain, because the seventeenth-century French philosopher René Descartes described that gland as the seat of the soul. That link is a modern blending of ideas; it is not part of the ancient Indian tradition, and it is not supported by science as an account of spiritual sight. But the core image, an eye that sees beyond appearances, is ancient and powerful.

The eyes of the Buddha

In the Kathmandu Valley of Nepal stand two of the most famous Buddhist monuments in the world, the great stupas of Boudhanath and Swayambhunath. A stupa is a dome-shaped shrine, often containing relics, around which pilgrims walk in prayer. Above the domes of these Nepali stupas rises a square tower, and on each of its four sides are painted a pair of large, calm, half-closed eyes. They are often called the Buddha eyes or the wisdom eyes. Between and below the eyes, where a nose would be, there is a curling sign that resembles a question mark; it is often explained as the Nepali numeral one, a sign of unity, or as a symbol of the single path to enlightenment. Above the eyes, on many stupas, there is also a third eye.

Because the eyes look out in all four directions, they suggest a gaze that takes in the whole world. But it is a gentle gaze, compassionate and serene, not threatening. In Buddhist teaching, the eye of wisdom sees things as they really are, without illusion. To have that sight is to be awake, which is what the word Buddha means.

The Buddha eyes are a good reminder that an all-seeing eye need not be frightening. For millions of people, the eye that sees everything is an eye of compassion. It sees suffering clearly so that suffering can be relieved.

Persia and the eye of the king

In the ancient Persian Empire, from the sixth to the fourth centuries BCE, the Greek historian Herodotus and other writers reported that the king had officials known as the King's Eye and the King's Ear. Their job was to watch over the provinces and report back on the behavior of governors and officials. Historians debate exactly how these offices worked, and whether "the King's Eye" was one person or a title held by many. But the phrase itself shows how naturally the eye became a metaphor for oversight and accountability in government. A just ruler was one who saw what was happening in his realm and corrected wrongs, even far from the capital.

Greece and Rome: the eye of the gods and the eye of envy

We have already met Argus of the hundred eyes and Helios, the sun who sees all. Greek and Roman culture also had a rich tradition of eye charms against the evil eye. Archaeologists have found Greek drinking cups, known as eye cups, from the sixth century BCE that have large eyes painted on their outer sides. When a person lifted the cup to drink, the eyes would face outward toward the other guests, like a mask. Scholars have suggested several possible meanings: protection against the evil eye, a playful mask effect, or a link to the god of wine, Dionysus. Probably more than one meaning was in play at the same time.

In Rome, phallic charms and eye images were used to ward off the envious gaze, especially for children, soldiers, and animals. Roman mosaics have been found that show an eye being attacked by animals, weapons, and other protective symbols, apparently meant to drive away the evil eye from a household. The Latin word for the evil eye, fascinum, gives us the English word fascinate, which originally meant to bewitch someone with a look.

The Norse god who gave an eye

Far to the north, in the mythology of the Norse peoples of Scandinavia, there is a very different and very moving eye story. Odin, the chief of the gods, was a seeker of wisdom. He was willing to pay any price to understand the world and its fate. According to the Old Norse poems and stories written down in Iceland in the thirteenth century, Odin went to the well of Mimir, whose waters gave wisdom, and asked to drink. Mimir demanded a price: one of Odin's eyes. Odin plucked out his eye and gave it up, and in return he drank from the well and gained great knowledge.

From then on, Odin was one-eyed. In paintings and carvings he is often shown with a hat pulled low over his face and a single eye. His sacrifice is a powerful image of the cost of wisdom. To see more deeply, he had to give up part of his ordinary sight. Odin also had two ravens, named Huginn and Muninn, usually translated as Thought and Memory, who flew over the world each day and returned to tell him everything they had seen. In this way, the one-eyed god saw everything.

There is something here for anyone who builds a business or a life on knowledge. Wisdom does not come for free. Learning the law, mastering a craft, building a skill that others will pay for: all of these cost something. Odin's single eye is not a sign of weakness. It is a sign of what he was willing to give.

The eye in Hebrew scripture

In the Hebrew Bible, God is described as seeing everything. There is no single eye symbol in ancient Israelite religion, which forbade images of God. But the language of divine sight is everywhere. In the Book of Genesis, Hagar, a servant woman fleeing into the wilderness, meets an angel and names God El Roi, "the God who sees me." In the Psalms, the writer asks where he could go to escape God's presence, and answers that neither the heights of heaven nor the depths of the earth nor the darkness itself could hide him. The Book of Proverbs says that the eyes of the Lord are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good. The prophet Zechariah has a vision of a stone with seven eyes, and of the seven eyes of the Lord that range through the whole earth.

These passages would become very important in Christian art, as we will see in the next chapter, when painters began to search for a way to show the all-seeing God without breaking the commandment against images.

The eye in Islamic tradition

Islamic tradition, too, forbids images of God, and Islamic art developed its genius instead in calligraphy, geometry, and pattern. But the Quran speaks often of God's knowledge and sight. One of the ninety-nine names of God in Islamic tradition is al-Basir, the All-Seeing. Another is al-Raqib, the Watchful. Another is al-Alim, the All-Knowing. The Quran says that no vision can grasp God, but that God grasps all vision. It speaks of God as the one who knows what is hidden and what is open.

In popular practice across the Islamic world, protective eye charms against the evil eye are common, as in neighboring cultures. Many Muslims also protect themselves from envy by saying masha'Allah, "what God has willed," when admiring something, so that the admiration does not carry the harm of envy. The idea is the same one we have met elsewhere: that a look can carry power, and that the right words or symbols can turn harm into blessing.

What the ancient eyes share

Looking back across these many traditions, a few common threads stand out.

First, the all-seeing eye is often linked with the sun. Shamash, Helios, Ra, and Surya are all sun gods who see everything. This makes sense: the sun lights the whole world, and in its light, nothing can hide. The rays around the eye in later art, including the Conscientia emblem, are the descendants of these solar eyes.

Second, the all-seeing eye is often linked with law and justice. Shamash gives Hammurabi his laws. The King's Eye in Persia watches over governors. The God of Israel sees the evil and the good. Because the eye sees everything, it can judge fairly. It cannot be fooled by appearances or bribed by flattery.

Third, the eye can be gentle as well as stern. The Buddha eyes of Nepal look out with compassion. The protective eye charms of the Mediterranean shield children and travelers. The eye of God in the Psalms is a presence that comforts as well as challenges.

Fourth, there is often a price for sight. Odin gives his eye for wisdom. Shiva's third eye opens only at a moment of great power. Inner vision is not cheap. It comes through sacrifice, discipline, and effort.

Fifth, and perhaps most important, the outer eye keeps turning into an inner one. The third eye of Indian tradition is an inner faculty. The wisdom eye of the Buddha is an awakened mind. The God who sees in secret, in many traditions, is known through the conscience. Again and again, people who began by imagining a watcher in the sky ended by recognizing a watcher in the heart.

That inward turn is exactly what the word Conscientia captures. In the next chapter, we will see how Christian artists in Europe brought these ideas together in a single image, the eye within a triangle, which would become the direct ancestor of the eye on the dollar bill and of the eye in our emblem.

Key Ideas

  • Across many ancient cultures, the all-seeing eye is linked with the sun, with light, and with law and justice.
  • The all-seeing eye can be gentle as well as stern, as the compassionate Buddha eyes of Nepal show.
  • Wisdom often has a price, as in the story of Odin giving his eye at Mimir's well.

Questions for Reflection

  1. What price have you paid for something you know? Was it worth it?
  2. Why do you think so many cultures connected the sun with justice?
  3. Is the idea of being seen by a higher power comforting, challenging, or both for you?

Chapter Four

The Eye of Providence

The eyes of the Lord are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good.
Proverbs 15:3

The eye in a triangle, surrounded by rays of light, is the image most people picture when they hear the phrase "all-seeing eye." It has a proper name: the Eye of Providence. It is not ancient. It does not come from Egypt. It grew up in Christian Europe, mostly between the fifteenth and eighteenth centuries, as artists and theologians looked for a way to represent God's watchful care over the world. Understanding where this image came from is the key to understanding the eye on the Great Seal of the United States, the eye in Masonic symbolism, and the eye in the Conscientia emblem.

What providence means

The word providence comes from the Latin providentia, which means foresight. It is built from pro, meaning ahead or before, and videre, meaning to see. Providence is literally seeing ahead. In Christian theology, providence is the belief that God not only created the world but continues to watch over it, care for it, and guide it toward its purpose. Nothing happens outside of God's knowledge. The fall of a sparrow, Jesus says in the Gospels, does not happen apart from the Father, and even the hairs of your head are all counted.

This is a comforting idea for many people. It means that the world is not ruled by chance, and that suffering and injustice are not the last word. It is also a challenging idea, because it means that nothing we do is hidden. Providence watches over us, and it also watches us. Both of these meanings, comfort and accountability, are carried by the Eye of Providence.

The problem of picturing God

For Christian artists, picturing God posed a real difficulty. The Hebrew scriptures forbid making images of God, and early Christians inherited much of that caution. Jesus could be shown, because Christians believe that in him God became a visible human being. The Holy Spirit could be shown as a dove, because the Gospels describe the Spirit descending on Jesus like a dove at his baptism. But God the Father was harder. In medieval art he was often represented by a hand reaching down from the clouds, a sign of his presence and power without showing his face. Later artists painted him as a venerable old man with a white beard, drawing on a vision in the Book of Daniel of the Ancient of Days. But many theologians and artists remained uneasy with such images.

The eye offered a solution. An eye could represent God's knowledge and presence without claiming to show what God looks like. It was abstract enough to avoid idolatry, yet vivid enough to speak to ordinary people. And scripture was full of references to God's eyes, as we saw in the last chapter. The eye was a natural choice.

The triangle of the Trinity

The triangle came from a different line of thought. Christian doctrine teaches that God is a Trinity: one God in three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This is a difficult idea to put into words, and for centuries theologians and teachers looked for images to help explain it. Saint Patrick, according to a well-known legend, used the three-leafed shamrock. Others used the image of three interlocking circles, or of a single flame burning in three candles.

The equilateral triangle, with three equal sides and three equal angles, became one of the most popular symbols of the Trinity. It is one shape, but it has three corners. Each side is equal to the others, just as, in Christian doctrine, each person of the Trinity is equal. A medieval diagram known as the Shield of the Trinity, which was widely used in England and France from the thirteenth century on, set out the doctrine in a triangle: the three persons at the corners, God at the center, and labels on the connecting lines explaining that each person is God, yet each is distinct from the others.

When artists placed an eye inside a triangle, they combined two ideas. The triangle said: this is the triune God. The eye said: this God sees everything. Together, they made a compact, powerful symbol of the God who watches over all creation.

The rays of glory

The third element of the classic Eye of Providence is the burst of light surrounding it. In Christian art, rays of light, called a glory, a gloria, or sometimes an aureole, are a sign of the divine. Halos around the heads of saints are a small form of the same idea. The rays say that this is holy, that this shines with a light not of this world. They also connect back to the ancient association between the all-seeing eye and the sun.

Often the eye and triangle are also set among clouds, showing that they belong to heaven. In many church decorations, the eye in the triangle with its rays appears at the very top of an altarpiece or high on a ceiling, looking down on the congregation below.

Early appearances

It is difficult to say exactly when the eye in a triangle first appeared, because many works of art have been lost and because the symbol seems to have developed gradually. But by the sixteenth century it was clearly in use. One of the most frequently cited early examples is the painting Supper at Emmaus by the Italian artist Jacopo Pontormo, completed in 1525 and now in the Uffizi Gallery in Florence. It shows the risen Jesus breaking bread with two disciples, who suddenly recognize him. Above Jesus's head, in a triangle of light, is a single staring eye. It is a startling image even today.

Over the following two centuries, the Eye of Providence spread across Catholic and Protestant Europe. It appeared in paintings, stained glass, engravings, book illustrations, and church architecture. Emblem books, a popular kind of illustrated book in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries that paired images with mottos and short poems, often used an eye in the sky to represent God's watchfulness. In the baroque churches of Central Europe, the eye in a triangle often gleams in gold above the altar, surrounded by sculpted clouds and rays.

Eyes in the emblem books

The emblem books are worth a closer look, because they are part of the ancestry of the very idea of an emblem. An emblem, in this older sense, was not a logo. It was a combination of three parts: a picture, a short motto, and a brief text explaining the meaning. The reader was meant to puzzle over the picture and the motto together and work out the moral lesson. The first famous emblem book was the Emblemata of the Italian lawyer Andrea Alciato, first printed in 1531, and it was followed by hundreds of others across Europe.

In these books, an eye often appears as a symbol of vigilance, watchfulness, or divine oversight. An eye on top of a scepter could represent wise government. An eye in the clouds could represent the providence of God. An eye on a hand could represent the idea that we should believe what we see for ourselves. The point is that, by the seventeenth century, educated Europeans were very used to reading eye images as symbols of virtues and ideas, not just as decorations.

The Conscientia emblem of Meechie's World Inc is, in a sense, an emblem in this old meaning as well as the modern one. It has a picture: the eye, the pyramid, and the book. It has mottos: Lux e tenebris and Iustitiam quaerimus. And it has a text explaining its meaning: this book.

The eye in the Protestant and Enlightenment world

By the eighteenth century, the Eye of Providence had become a symbol with meaning well beyond the walls of the church. During the period known as the Enlightenment, many thinkers in Europe and America moved away from traditional religious doctrines toward a more general belief in a creator who had made the world according to rational laws. This belief is often called deism. Deists did not always believe in miracles or in the Trinity, but many of them did believe in providence, in a God who had designed the world wisely and who watched over human affairs in a general way.

For people like this, the Eye of Providence was a perfect symbol. It could be read as Christian, but it did not have to be. It said that the universe had a wise and watchful creator, without saying too much about the details. This is part of why it was so attractive to the founders of the United States and to the Freemasons of the eighteenth century, as the next two chapters will explain.

The eye on everyday objects

In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the Eye of Providence also appeared on all kinds of everyday objects. It was printed on certificates, carved on gravestones, painted on the ceilings of public buildings, and engraved on medals and coins. On gravestones, it reminded passersby that God sees and remembers the dead. On certificates and official documents, it suggested that the agreement was made under God's eye and that the parties were bound in conscience to keep it. On public buildings, it said that the government itself was answerable to a higher power.

This use on documents is particularly worth noticing. When an eye appears at the top of a certificate or a charter, it acts as a kind of witness. It says: this agreement was made in good faith, and it is seen. That is very close to the purpose of the eye in the Conscientia emblem, which appears at the top of every document Meechie's World Inc prepares. The eye over the page is a promise of honesty.

Reading the Eye of Providence rightly

Because the Eye of Providence has been so widely used, and because it later became a target of conspiracy theories, it is easy to lose sight of what it meant to the people who made it. For the painters of Renaissance Italy, the craftsmen of baroque Germany, and the engravers of eighteenth-century England, the eye in the triangle did not stand for a secret society or a hidden plan. It stood for something very public and very widely shared: the belief that God sees all, cares for all, and will judge all fairly.

It is a symbol of watchfulness, not of spying. Of providence, not of control. Of light, not of darkness. When we see it in a church or on an old certificate, the right response is not suspicion but reflection: am I living as though my actions are seen? Would I be comfortable if everything I did in private were brought into the light?

That question is the beating heart of the word conscience. It is the question the Conscientia emblem asks every time it appears.

From the church to the seal

In 1776, a group of men in Philadelphia were given the job of designing a seal for a new nation. One of the images they considered, and that would eventually find its way onto the reverse of the Great Seal of the United States and from there onto the one-dollar bill, was the Eye of Providence. How that happened, and what it meant, is the subject of the next chapter.

Key Ideas

  • The Eye of Providence, an eye in a triangle with rays, developed in Christian Europe from about the fifteenth to the eighteenth century.
  • It combines the eye of God's watchful care, the triangle of the Trinity, and the rays of divine glory.
  • On documents and certificates, the eye acts as a witness that the agreement is made in good faith.

Questions for Reflection

  1. What does the word providence, seeing ahead, suggest about how we should plan our own lives?
  2. Why might artists have chosen an eye to represent God rather than a human figure?
  3. What agreements in your life would you want to be made under a watchful eye?

Chapter Five

The Great Seal of the United States

The pyramid signifies Strength and Duration.
Charles Thomson, 1782

Pull a one-dollar bill out of your pocket and turn it over. On the left side, inside a circle, you will see an unfinished pyramid of thirteen steps, sitting on bare ground. Floating above it, in a triangle surrounded by rays of light, is a single eye. Above the eye are the Latin words ANNUIT COEPTIS. Beneath the pyramid is a banner with the words NOVUS ORDO SECLORUM, and on the bottom step of the pyramid, in Roman numerals, the date MDCCLXXVI: 1776.

This image is the reverse side of the Great Seal of the United States. It is probably the most widely reproduced picture of an eye in the world, printed on billions of banknotes. It is also the source of more myths and misunderstandings than almost any other national symbol. This chapter tells the real story of how it came to be.

A seal for a new nation

In the eighteenth century, a seal was an essential tool of government. Treaties, commissions, and important official documents were authenticated by pressing a metal die into wax or paper. The seal proved that a document was genuine and that it carried the authority of the state. A new country needed its own seal as urgently as it needed a flag.

On the afternoon of July 4, 1776, the same day the Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Independence, it appointed a committee to design a seal for the United States. The members were three of the most famous men in America: Benjamin Franklin, John Adams, and Thomas Jefferson. They consulted an artist living in Philadelphia, Pierre Eugène du Simitière, a Swiss-born painter and collector who had experience designing seals and coats of arms.

Each man had his own ideas. Franklin proposed a scene from the Book of Exodus: Moses raising his hand over the Red Sea as the waters close over Pharaoh's army, with rays from a pillar of fire shining on Moses, and the motto "Rebellion to Tyrants is Obedience to God." Jefferson suggested the children of Israel in the wilderness, led by a cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night, and on the other side the Saxon chiefs Hengist and Horsa, legendary ancestors of the English. Adams suggested a scene from classical mythology, the Judgment of Hercules, showing the hero choosing between the hard path of virtue and the easy path of pleasure.

Du Simitière's own proposal was a shield bearing the symbols of the six European nations from which most Americans had come, supported by the figures of Liberty and Justice, with the motto E Pluribus Unum, "out of many, one." At the top of his design, as a crest, he placed the Eye of Providence in a radiant triangle.

The committee reported back to Congress on August 20, 1776, with a combination of these ideas: du Simitière's shield and supporters, crowned with the Eye of Providence, on the front, and Franklin's Moses scene on the back. Congress did not adopt it. But two elements of this first design would survive into the final seal: the motto E Pluribus Unum, and the Eye of Providence.

The second and third committees

Congress returned to the question in 1780, with a second committee made up of James Lovell, John Morin Scott, and William Churchill Houston, who consulted Francis Hopkinson, a lawyer, writer, musician, and designer from Philadelphia. Hopkinson is often credited with a role in designing the American flag. This committee proposed thirteen red and white stripes, a constellation of thirteen stars, and an olive branch as a symbol of peace. Again Congress did not adopt the design, but again some of its elements survived.

Hopkinson had already used another important image. In 1778 he designed the fifty-dollar note of the Continental currency, the paper money issued by Congress during the war. On it he placed an unfinished pyramid with the Latin word PERENNIS, meaning everlasting or enduring. This is the first known appearance of the unfinished pyramid in an American national design.

In 1782 a third committee was appointed, made up of Arthur Middleton, Elias Boudinot, and Arthur Lee, with a young Philadelphia lawyer and scholar of heraldry named William Barton as consultant. Barton produced a detailed design. For the reverse of the seal, he proposed a pyramid of thirteen steps, with the Eye of Providence in a triangle above it, and two mottos: Deo Favente, "with God favoring," and Perennis.

Charles Thomson pulls it together

Congress then handed all the committees' work to Charles Thomson, the Secretary of the Continental Congress. Thomson was not an artist, but he was a scholar of Latin and Greek and a man with a clear sense of what the seal needed to say. Working in June 1782, he took the best elements from the earlier designs and combined them into the seal we know today.

For the front, or obverse, Thomson chose an American bald eagle with its wings spread, holding an olive branch of thirteen leaves in one talon and a bundle of thirteen arrows in the other, representing peace and war. On the eagle's breast he placed a shield of thirteen stripes. In its beak, a scroll bears the motto E Pluribus Unum. Above its head, a glory of light breaks through clouds around a constellation of thirteen stars.

For the reverse, Thomson kept Barton's pyramid and the Eye of Providence, but he changed the mottos. Above the eye he placed ANNUIT COEPTIS. Below the pyramid he placed NOVUS ORDO SECLORUM. He kept the date MDCCLXXVI at the base of the pyramid. Barton then made some final adjustments to the drawing, and on June 20, 1782, Congress adopted the design.

What Thomson said it meant

We do not have to guess what the designers intended, because Charles Thomson wrote an explanation that he submitted to Congress along with the design. Of the reverse, he wrote that the pyramid signifies strength and duration, that the eye over it and the motto allude to the many signal interpositions of providence in favor of the American cause, that the date underneath is that of the Declaration of Independence, and that the words under it signify the beginning of the new American era, which commences from that date.

This is about as clear as an explanation can be. The pyramid is a symbol of strength and of a structure meant to last for ages. It is unfinished because the nation was new and still being built, and because more states would be added. The thirteen steps are the thirteen original states. The eye is the Eye of Providence, the watchful care of God, which the founders believed had helped them through the war. The mottos say that providence has favored the undertaking and that a new era has begun.

There is no mention of secret societies, hidden knowledge, or plans to rule the world. The meaning is public, patriotic, and religious in the broad, eighteenth-century sense that most Americans of the time would have recognized.

The mottos explained

The two Latin mottos on the reverse are both adapted from the Roman poet Virgil, whom educated people in the eighteenth century read in school.

Annuit coeptis means "he has favored our undertakings" or "he has approved our beginnings." The subject is understood to be God, or providence. The phrase echoes lines in Virgil's poems where a speaker prays to Jupiter to favor a bold undertaking. Thomson explained that the motto, together with the eye, alludes to the interventions of providence on behalf of the American cause.

Novus ordo seclorum means "a new order of the ages." It is adapted from a line in Virgil's Fourth Eclogue, which speaks of a great order of the ages being born anew. Thomson used it to mean the start of a new American era beginning in 1776.

This second motto is very often mistranslated as "new world order," a phrase that sounds sinister and that has been used by conspiracy theorists to suggest that the dollar bill announces a plan for global domination. But seclorum, or saeculorum in classical spelling, does not mean "world." It means "of the ages" or "of the generations." The phrase is about time, not territory. It means a new chapter in history, not a new world government.

The reverse that was never cut

Here is a fact that surprises many people: for over a century and a half, the reverse of the Great Seal was almost never seen. A seal, after all, is used to make impressions on documents, and a document only needs one side. Congress had a die made of the obverse, with the eagle, and that die was used to seal official documents. But no die of the reverse was cut. The pyramid and the eye existed on paper, in the official description and in a few drawings and publications, but they were not in everyday use.

That changed in the 1930s. According to the account later given by Henry A. Wallace, who was Secretary of Agriculture under President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Wallace came across a picture of the reverse of the seal in a State Department publication on the history of the seal, and was struck by the motto Novus Ordo Seclorum, which he took to suggest a "New Deal of the ages," fitting the spirit of Roosevelt's economic program. Wallace brought it to Roosevelt, who liked the idea of placing both sides of the seal on the currency. Roosevelt himself made some changes to the proposed layout, including moving the reverse to the left side of the bill and the obverse to the right, and adding the words "The Great Seal of the United States" beneath both.

The new one-dollar bill, with both sides of the Great Seal on its back, appeared in 1935. It has carried them ever since. Because of this, the eye above the pyramid, which had been nearly forgotten for a hundred and fifty years, became one of the most familiar images in the world almost overnight.

The Masonic question

Both Roosevelt and Wallace were Freemasons. Benjamin Franklin, on the first seal committee, was a prominent Freemason. These facts have led many people to believe that the Great Seal is a Masonic symbol, and that the eye above the pyramid was placed there by Masons as a secret sign.

The evidence does not support this. The eye was proposed by du Simitière, who is not known to have been a Mason, and it was carried into the final design by William Barton and Charles Thomson, neither of whom is known to have been a Mason. Franklin, the one confirmed Mason on the first committee, proposed the Moses design, not the eye. The design of the reverse dates from 1782, and as the next chapter will show, the all-seeing eye only became a common and widely published Masonic symbol in the years after that, especially after 1797. If anything, the Masons and the designers of the Great Seal were both drawing on the same well: the widespread eighteenth-century use of the Eye of Providence in Christian and Enlightenment art.

As for Roosevelt and Wallace in 1935, they put an existing national symbol on the currency. They did not design it. The fact that they were Masons is interesting, but it does not change what the seal meant to the people who created it.

Why the unfinished pyramid matters

There is something powerful about a nation choosing an unfinished building as its symbol. Most national seals show something complete: a crowned shield, a lion, a castle. The American reverse shows a structure still under construction. The top is missing. The work is not done.

This is a fitting image for any young enterprise. A nation, a family, a business, a life: all of these are built step by step, on a foundation laid by those who came before, and none of them is ever truly finished. The eye above the pyramid watches the work as it goes on. It does not replace the missing capstone; it hovers in the space where the capstone would be, as if to say that the completion of the work belongs to providence, or to the future.

The Conscientia emblem of Meechie's World Inc keeps this idea but changes its setting. In our emblem, too, the eye shines in a capstone just above a pyramid of stone courses. But the capstone sits close, almost touching, glowing with its own light, and the whole pyramid rests on an open book. That is a different statement. It says that the top of the work is within reach, that conscience is the crown of the structure rather than a distant hope, and that the whole building, from its lowest course to its shining peak, stands on knowledge, on law, and on the written record.

The eye and the dollar

There is one more lesson in the story of the Great Seal. Because the eye ended up on money, many people now associate it with wealth, banks, and financial power. Some see that as sinister. But consider what the designers actually put on the bill: an eye that watches, and a reminder that the nation's success depends on providence, on strength, and on the endurance of its foundations, not on money alone.

There is something fitting about an image of watchful conscience appearing on money, of all things. Money is one of the places where people are most tempted to cut corners, to cheat, to hide. An eye on a banknote says: this is seen. Every exchange, every payment, every promise to pay is made under a watchful eye. For a business like Meechie's World Inc, which handles people's payments, documents, and trust, that is exactly the right reminder.

In the next chapter, we will turn to the Freemasons, who adopted the all-seeing eye in their own way, and whose use of it gave the symbol much of its modern mystique.

  • Novus ordo seclorum means a new order of the ages, not a new world order.
  • The reverse of the seal was rarely seen until it was placed on the one-dollar bill in 1935.
