Chapter Six

The Eye and the Craft: Freemasonry

Our thoughts, words and actions may be hidden from the eyes of man.
Thomas Smith Webb, The Freemason's Monitor, 1797

No group is more closely associated with the all-seeing eye in the popular imagination than the Freemasons. The eye appears on Masonic aprons, certificates, jewelry, temple walls, and charts. It has become, for many people, the very emblem of Freemasonry, and from there of secret brotherhoods in general. This chapter explains who the Freemasons are, how and when they adopted the eye, what it means in Masonic teaching, and why the Conscientia emblem draws on this tradition without belonging to it.

Who are the Freemasons?

Freemasonry is a fraternal organization, a brotherhood whose members meet in local groups called lodges. Its origins lie in the guilds of stonemasons who built the cathedrals, castles, and other great buildings of medieval Europe. These working masons, especially in Scotland and England, had their own organizations, rules, and customs, including ways of recognizing each other and passing on the secrets of their trade.

Over the course of the seventeenth century, these lodges began to admit members who were not working stonemasons at all: gentlemen, scholars, merchants, and others who were drawn to the lodges' fellowship and to the moral lessons that could be taught through the tools and practices of building. These new members were called accepted or speculative masons, as opposed to operative masons who actually worked with stone. Gradually, the speculative side took over.

The modern history of Freemasonry is usually dated to 1717, when four lodges in London came together to form a Grand Lodge, a central body to oversee them. Other Grand Lodges followed in Ireland, Scotland, and elsewhere. During the eighteenth century, Freemasonry spread rapidly across Europe and the American colonies. Many prominent figures of the age were Masons, including George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, Paul Revere, and the composer Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart.

Freemasonry describes itself as a system of morality veiled in allegory and illustrated by symbols. Members progress through degrees, the first three of which are Entered Apprentice, Fellow Craft, and Master Mason. Each degree involves a ceremony in which lessons are taught through drama and symbolism. Masons are expected to believe in a Supreme Being, but the organization does not ask its members to belong to any particular religion. Lodges are forbidden to discuss religion and politics in a divisive way.

Prince Hall Freemasonry

Any account of Freemasonry in America must include the story of Prince Hall. In 1775, in Boston, a free Black man named Prince Hall and fourteen other free Black men were initiated into Freemasonry by a lodge attached to a British army regiment. When the regiment left, Hall and his brothers were permitted to meet as a lodge but were refused full recognition by the white Masonic authorities in Massachusetts. Hall applied directly to the Grand Lodge of England, which in 1784 issued a warrant for African Lodge No. 459. The warrant, after delays at sea, reached Boston in 1787.

From this beginning grew Prince Hall Freemasonry, which has been one of the most important institutions in Black American life for more than two centuries. Prince Hall lodges provided fellowship, mutual aid, leadership training, and a network of support at a time when Black Americans were excluded from most public institutions. Many leaders of the civil rights movement and of Black business, politics, and culture were Prince Hall Masons. Prince Hall himself was an abolitionist who petitioned the Massachusetts legislature to end slavery and to provide schools for Black children.

The story of Prince Hall is a reminder that symbols like the all-seeing eye have been carried, in America, not only by the powerful but by people fighting for recognition, dignity, and justice. That history matters to a company that has chosen the words Iustitiam quaerimus, we seek justice, as part of its crest.

The symbols of the lodge

Freemasonry uses a large number of symbols, most of them drawn from the tools and architecture of building. The best known is the square and compasses, usually shown interlocked, often with the letter G in the center. The square, used to test right angles, teaches that Masons should square their actions by the rules of virtue. The compasses, used to draw circles, teach that they should keep their desires within due bounds. The letter G is usually explained as standing for God, for geometry, or for both.

Other symbols include the level, which teaches equality; the plumb, which teaches uprightness; the trowel, which spreads the cement of brotherly love; the twenty-four-inch gauge, which represents the twenty-four hours of the day to be divided among work, rest, and service; the rough and the perfect ashlar, stones representing the person in his natural state and as improved by education; the two pillars, named Boaz and Jachin after the pillars of King Solomon's Temple; the beehive, a symbol of industry; the anchor and ark; the hourglass and scythe, reminders of mortality; and the sun, moon, and stars.

Among these symbols, alongside the square and compasses and the letter G, is the all-seeing eye.

When the eye entered the lodge

Contrary to what many people assume, the all-seeing eye was not part of the earliest Masonic symbolism. It does not appear in the earliest records of the London Grand Lodge in the 1720s and 1730s. It seems to have entered Masonic use gradually during the second half of the eighteenth century, borrowed from the general Christian and Enlightenment use of the Eye of Providence described in Chapter Four.

The key moment in America came in 1797, when a Masonic writer and lecturer named Thomas Smith Webb published a book called The Freemason's Monitor, or Illustrations of Masonry. Webb's book was a handbook of Masonic ritual and lectures, and it became enormously influential in the United States, shaping the way Masonry was practiced for generations. In it, Webb included the all-seeing eye among the emblems of the Master Mason degree, with an explanation that is still recited in many lodges.

According to Webb, although our thoughts, words, and actions may be hidden from the eyes of other people, the All-Seeing Eye, which the sun, moon, and stars obey, and under whose watchful care even comets perform their revolutions, sees into the innermost recesses of the human heart, and will reward us according to our merits.

This explanation makes the meaning of the Masonic eye very clear. It is not a sign that Masons see everything. It is a reminder to the Mason that he himself is seen. It is a lesson in conscience. A Mason is meant to act rightly not because other people are watching, but because God sees everything, even what is hidden in the heart.

In 1819, another American Masonic writer, Jeremy Ladd Cross, published The True Masonic Chart, a book of illustrations that gave Masons visual images to go with Webb's lectures. Cross's engravings included the all-seeing eye, and his chart spread the image widely among American lodges. From then on, the eye became a standard part of Masonic imagery in the United States, appearing on aprons, certificates, and lodge decorations.

The eye and the pyramid in Masonry

It is worth noting that the classic Masonic eye is usually shown in a cloud or a burst of light, sometimes in a triangle, but not usually above a pyramid. The combination of the eye with the pyramid comes from the Great Seal, not from Masonic tradition. Freemasons, being builders, have plenty of architectural symbols, but the pyramid is not one of the central ones in the core degrees. The confusion between the two traditions comes partly from the fact that both used the Eye of Providence in the same era, and partly from the later presence of Masons such as Roosevelt and Wallace in the story of the dollar bill.

Secrecy and suspicion

Freemasonry has always kept some of its rituals, passwords, and signs of recognition private. Members take obligations not to reveal them. This secrecy, harmless in itself, has made Masons a target of suspicion for almost three hundred years. In 1738, Pope Clement XII issued a decree forbidding Catholics from joining the Masons, and the Catholic Church has maintained its opposition in various forms ever since.

In the United States, a wave of anti-Masonic feeling swept the country after 1826, when a man named William Morgan of Batavia, New York, who had announced plans to publish an exposé of Masonic rituals, disappeared and was widely believed to have been murdered by Masons. The scandal led to the formation of the Anti-Masonic Party, the first significant third party in American politics, which held the first national nominating convention in 1831. Many lodges closed during this period, though Freemasonry later recovered.

The combination of secrecy, prominent members, and a mysterious-looking symbol made it easy for critics to imagine that the Masons were up to something sinister. The all-seeing eye, which to Masons was a humble reminder of their own accountability, came to look to outsiders like a sign of hidden power. This misunderstanding feeds directly into the myths discussed in the next chapter.

What the Masonic eye teaches

Setting aside the suspicions, the Masonic teaching about the eye is a profound one, and it is worth taking seriously. It says that a person of good character behaves the same way whether or not anyone is watching. It says that the real test of morality is not what we do in public, where our reputation is at stake, but what we do in private, where only our conscience sees. It says that we will be judged, in the end, by what is in our hearts.

These ideas are not secret, and they are not unique to Freemasonry. They are shared by almost every religious and ethical tradition in the world. But the Masons gave them a vivid symbol and a memorable form of words, and their influence helped make the all-seeing eye a symbol of conscience for millions of people.

The Conscientia emblem and the Craft

The emblem of Meechie's World Inc is not a Masonic emblem. It does not use the square and compasses, the letter G, or any of the private signs of the lodge, and it makes no claim to Masonic authority. The company is not a lodge, and the emblem does not imply that anyone associated with it holds any Masonic degree.

But the emblem does share something important with the Masonic teaching about the eye. The word beneath it, Conscientia, says exactly what Webb's lecture says: that we are seen, that what is hidden will be known, and that our actions should be worthy of that sight. Meechie's World Inc publishes a range of books, including work that explores Masonic history and symbolism, and the company respects the long tradition of builders, Black and white, who have used the eye as a reminder to live uprightly.

The Masons teach their members to be builders of character, to work on themselves as a mason works on rough stone until it becomes a perfect ashlar, smooth and square and ready for its place in the wall. That is a good image for any business, too. A company is built one decision at a time. Each honest transaction is a stone laid true. Each kept promise squares the wall. And the eye above it all watches to see whether the work is done well.

In the next chapter, we will turn to the darker side of the eye's reputation: the conspiracy theories that have grown up around it, and the truth behind them.

Chapter Seven

Myths, Fears and Misreadings

Come, let us reason together.
Isaiah 1:18

Type "all-seeing eye" into any search engine or video app and you will quickly find yourself in a world of shadows. Within a few clicks, you will be told that the eye is the mark of the Illuminati, a secret society that controls the world's governments, banks, media, and music industry. You will see compilations of celebrities making triangle shapes with their hands, covering one eye in photographs, or wearing jewelry with pyramids and eyes. You will hear that the dollar bill is a coded message announcing a plan for a new world order. You will be warned that anyone who uses the eye in a logo is either a member of the secret society or a dupe of it.

A book about an emblem built around the all-seeing eye has a responsibility to deal with these claims honestly. This chapter does that. It does not mock the people who believe these things. Many of them are sincerely trying to understand why the world seems so unfair, why power seems so concentrated, and why ordinary people seem to have so little control over their lives. Those are real questions. But the answers offered by the Illuminati myth are not true, and believing them can lead people away from the real causes of injustice and the real tools for fighting it.

The real Illuminati

The Illuminati was a real organization. It was founded on May 1, 1776, in Bavaria, a region in what is now southern Germany, by a young professor of law at the University of Ingolstadt named Adam Weishaupt. Its full name was the Order of the Illuminati, from the Latin illuminati, meaning enlightened ones. Weishaupt was a man of the Enlightenment who opposed the influence of the Catholic Church, particularly the Jesuits, over education and public life in Bavaria. He wanted to create a secret network of educated men who would promote reason, secular learning, and moral improvement, and who would gradually gain influence in society.

The order was small at first, and it grew mainly by recruiting from Masonic lodges, whose structure of degrees and secret rituals it imitated. A German nobleman named Adolph Freiherr Knigge helped to expand it in the early 1780s. At its height, the order had perhaps two thousand members, mostly in German-speaking lands, including some aristocrats, officials, and intellectuals.

Its life was short. Between 1784 and 1785, the ruler of Bavaria, the Elector Karl Theodor, issued a series of decrees banning secret societies, including the Illuminati specifically. The government seized the order's papers and published some of them to expose it. Weishaupt lost his position and fled. By the end of the 1780s, the Bavarian Illuminati had effectively ceased to exist as an organization.

Two facts are especially important for our story. First, the Illuminati did not use the all-seeing eye as its symbol. The emblem most associated with the order was the Owl of Minerva, the bird of the Roman goddess of wisdom, perched on an open book. Second, the Illuminati had nothing to do with the design of the Great Seal of the United States. The eye on the seal was proposed in Philadelphia in 1776 by a Swiss-born artist and finalized in 1782 by Charles Thomson, a Pennsylvania scholar, for reasons Thomson explained in writing, as we saw in Chapter Five. The coincidence that the Illuminati was founded in 1776, the same year that appears on the seal, is just that: a coincidence. 1776 is on the seal because it is the year of the Declaration of Independence.

How the myth was born

If the Illuminati disappeared in the 1780s, how did it come to be seen as an all-powerful secret government? The answer begins with the French Revolution.

In 1789, revolution broke out in France. Within a few years, the king had been executed, the old aristocracy overthrown, the Church attacked, and Europe plunged into war. Many people, especially conservatives, were horrified and bewildered. How could such a catastrophe have happened? Some looked for a hidden hand.

In 1797 and 1798, two books appeared that offered an answer. One was by a French Jesuit priest, the Abbé Augustin Barruel, titled Memoirs Illustrating the History of Jacobinism. The other was by a Scottish scientist, John Robison, titled Proofs of a Conspiracy. Both argued that the French Revolution had been secretly planned and carried out by a conspiracy of Freemasons, philosophers, and especially the Illuminati, who had supposedly survived their suppression in Bavaria and gone underground.

These books were widely read. In the United States, they caused a panic in 1798 and 1799, when some ministers, notably the Reverend Jedidiah Morse in New England, warned from the pulpit that the Illuminati had infiltrated America. George Washington, himself a Freemason, received a copy of Robison's book and replied in a letter that he had heard much of the plan of the Illuminati, but that he did not believe the lodges of Freemasons in the United States had been contaminated by its principles. The panic faded.

But the idea had been planted: that a secret society, hidden behind ordinary institutions, was steering world events. Over the next two centuries, that idea would be revived again and again, attached to different groups depending on who was afraid of whom.

A dangerous pattern

It must be said plainly that conspiracy theories about secret world governments have often been used to spread hatred against particular groups of people. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the myth of a hidden conspiracy controlling banks, governments, and the press was very often aimed at Jewish people. A notorious forgery called The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, first published in Russia in 1903, claimed to reveal a Jewish plan for world domination. It was proven to be a fake, partly plagiarized from an earlier French satire that had nothing to do with Jews, but it was spread widely and used to justify persecution and, ultimately, genocide.

Modern Illuminati theories often borrow, sometimes knowingly and sometimes not, from this same tradition. That is one more reason to approach them with great care. A theory that tells you a hidden group is responsible for all your problems is a theory that can be turned against your neighbors.

From satire to belief

The modern explosion of interest in the Illuminati has an odd origin: a joke. In the 1960s, a group of American writers and pranksters created a mock religion called Discordianism, which included elaborate satirical stories about the Illuminati. Two writers connected to this group, Robert Shea and Robert Anton Wilson, wrote a sprawling comic science-fiction trilogy called Illuminatus!, published in 1975, which parodied conspiracy theories by piling them all together in absurd combinations. The eye in the pyramid featured prominently.

The trilogy became a cult classic, and many readers missed or ignored the joke. Elements of its parody were absorbed into genuine conspiracy thinking. Later, with the arrival of the internet, Illuminati theories spread faster than ever before. In the 2000s and 2010s, they became especially attached to the music industry, with claims that famous rappers and pop stars were members or puppets of the Illuminati, and that their videos and album covers were full of coded signs.

Why the eye seems everywhere

One reason the Illuminati myth is so persuasive is that the eye and the triangle really are everywhere. Once you start looking for them, you see them constantly. Triangles are among the simplest shapes in geometry; they appear in countless logos, buildings, and designs for purely practical reasons. Eyes, as we saw in Chapter One, are among the most attention-grabbing images there are, which is why designers use them. Covering one eye in a photograph is a common pose in fashion photography because it creates a striking, asymmetrical image. Artists use the eye in the pyramid precisely because it has a mysterious reputation; it sells.

Psychologists have a name for the human tendency to see meaningful patterns in random information: apophenia. Our brains are pattern-finding machines, and that is usually a good thing. It helps us learn, predict, and survive. But it also means that, if we go looking for a hidden pattern, we will almost always find one, whether or not it is really there. When a theory tells us that every eye and every triangle is a sign, and then we see eyes and triangles everywhere, the theory seems confirmed. But all we have really confirmed is that eyes and triangles are common.

Real power, real accountability

Here is the most important point. The world really does contain concentrations of power. Wealth really is unequally distributed. Governments, corporations, and powerful individuals really do sometimes act in secret, break the law, and harm ordinary people. These are not myths. They are documented in court records, investigative journalism, government reports, and history books.

The trouble with the Illuminati myth is not that it notices power. It is that it misidentifies it. By pointing at a fantasy, it draws attention away from the real, traceable, accountable people and institutions that actually make decisions. You cannot sue the Illuminati. You cannot vote out the Illuminati. You cannot file a grievance, a motion, or a freedom-of-information request against the Illuminati. But you can do all of those things against real officials, real companies, and real agencies.

This is where the mission of Meechie's World Inc connects directly to the symbol in its emblem. The company helps people prepare legal documents to represent themselves in court. It helps people who are incarcerated, and their families, raise grievances about real conditions. It helps small businesses and artists get their work seen. All of this is about facing real power with real tools: paper, evidence, law, and persistence. The eye in our emblem does not stand for a secret elite. It stands for the opposite: the conviction that power must be seen, documented, and held to account.

Reclaiming the eye

There is a long tradition of reclaiming symbols that have been misunderstood or misused. The eye belongs to no single group. It belonged to the Egyptian priests and the Babylonian judges, to the Buddhist monks of Nepal and the painters of Florence, to the founders who designed the Great Seal and the Prince Hall Masons who fought for recognition. It belongs to anyone who has ever felt the weight of conscience.

When Meechie's World Inc chose the eye for its emblem, it chose it with full knowledge of the myths that surround it. The company does not hide from those myths. It answers them. The eye in the Conscientia emblem is placed above an open book, not a closed one, because what it stands for is meant to be read by everyone. It is surrounded by light, because what it reveals is meant to be brought out of darkness. And it is labeled, plainly, in Latin and in English, so that no one has to guess: Conscientia. Conscience. Knowing together.

Questions to ask

When you encounter a claim about secret symbols or hidden conspiracies, a few questions can help you think it through.

What is the evidence, and where does it come from? Is it a document, a court record, an eyewitness, or just a picture with a circle drawn around it?

Who benefits from my believing this? Is someone selling books, videos, or products on the back of the claim?

Does the claim explain everything? A theory that explains every possible event, so that any evidence against it can be twisted into evidence for it, is a sign of trouble. Real explanations have limits.

Who is the theory blaming? If it points at a whole group of people defined by their religion, race, or origin, be very careful.

What can I actually do? A good understanding of a problem usually suggests real steps to address it. A theory that leaves you feeling powerless and afraid is not serving you.

These are the same questions any good paralegal, journalist, or judge would ask. They are the questions of a conscience that wants the truth.

  • Illuminati myths grew after the French Revolution and have often been used to spread hatred against groups of people.

Chapter Eight

The Pyramid: Foundation and Ascent

Man fears time, but time fears the pyramids.
Arab proverb

Of all the shapes human beings have built, none has lasted like the pyramid. The Great Pyramid of Giza, built for the Egyptian king Khufu around 2560 BCE, was the tallest structure made by human hands for nearly four thousand years. It has survived earthquakes, floods, invasions, stone robbers, and the slow grinding of desert winds. It was already ancient when the Greek historian Herodotus visited it in the fifth century BCE. It was ancient when Julius Caesar came to Egypt, ancient when the Arab armies arrived in the seventh century, ancient when Napoleon's soldiers stood before it in 1798. It is still there.

It is no wonder that the pyramid became a symbol of permanence, strength, and the ambition to build something that outlasts a single life. In the Conscientia emblem, the pyramid holds the eye and rests on the open book. This chapter explains why.

Why a pyramid?

The pyramid is, first of all, an engineering answer to a simple problem: how do you build something very tall out of heavy stone without it falling down? The answer is to make it wide at the base and narrow at the top. Each layer rests securely on the larger layer beneath it. The weight is carried downward and outward into the ground. A pyramid is the most stable shape a large stone structure can take. It does not need columns, beams, or arches. Gravity holds it together.

This is why piles of material naturally form a pyramid or cone shape. Pour sand, grain, or gravel onto the ground, and it will heap itself into a cone. Many cultures that had no contact with Egypt built pyramid-like structures for the same practical reason: the ziggurats of Mesopotamia, the step pyramids of Mesoamerica, the burial mounds of many lands, and the temple towers of Southeast Asia. The pyramid is, in a sense, the shape that the earth itself suggests.

The Egyptian pyramids

The Egyptian pyramids developed over several centuries. Early Egyptian kings were buried in flat-topped rectangular tombs made of mud brick, called mastabas. Around 2650 BCE, the architect Imhotep, working for King Djoser, stacked six mastaba-like layers of stone on top of one another, each smaller than the one below, to create the Step Pyramid at Saqqara. It was the first large building in history made entirely of cut stone.

Later kings refined the idea. King Sneferu experimented with several pyramids, including the famous Bent Pyramid at Dahshur, whose builders changed the angle of the sides partway up, apparently because the original angle was too steep and unstable. Sneferu's son Khufu then built the Great Pyramid at Giza, with smooth sides that originally rose at an angle of about fifty-one degrees to a point nearly 147 meters, or about 481 feet, high. Two more great pyramids followed at Giza, built for Khafre and Menkaure.

The pyramids were tombs, but they were more than tombs. They were enormous machines for the king's eternal life. Egyptian religion taught that the king, after death, would join the gods and travel with the sun. The pyramid shape may have represented the rays of the sun streaming down from the sky, a stairway for the king's spirit to ascend, or the primeval mound of earth that rose from the waters of chaos at the beginning of creation. Egyptologists continue to debate exactly which of these meanings was most important, and most likely all of them were present to some degree.

At the top of each pyramid sat a capstone, the pyramidion. As we saw in Chapter Two, these capstones were sometimes covered with gold or electrum so that they would be the first part of the pyramid to catch the rising sun. The Egyptians associated the pyramidion with the benben stone, a sacred stone kept at the temple of the sun in the city of Heliopolis, which represented the first piece of land to emerge at creation and on which the first light of the sun shone.

Who built them?

For a long time, many people believed that the pyramids were built by armies of slaves driven by the whip. This image owes a great deal to Hollywood movies and to a misreading of ancient sources. Archaeological discoveries since the 1990s, especially the excavation of workers' villages and cemeteries near Giza, have changed that picture. The workers who built the pyramids appear to have been organized teams of Egyptian laborers, some skilled craftsmen working year-round and others seasonal workers, perhaps farmers serving during the months when the Nile flood covered their fields. They lived in organized settlements, were fed with bread, beer, and meat, received medical care, and were buried with honor near the monuments they built. Some of their tombs include inscriptions proudly naming the work gangs they belonged to, with names like "Friends of Khufu."

This is worth remembering. The pyramid was not just the monument of a king. It was the achievement of thousands of ordinary people working together, organized and fed and proud of what they made. Every block was set by human hands. A pyramid is a picture of collective effort.

The pyramid as a symbol

Over the centuries, the pyramid became a symbol in its own right, separate from Egypt. Roman visitors to Egypt admired the pyramids, and at least one wealthy Roman, a magistrate named Gaius Cestius, built himself a pyramid-shaped tomb in Rome around 12 BCE. It still stands near the city's Porta San Paolo. During the Renaissance and especially in the eighteenth century, European artists and architects revived the pyramid as a symbol of eternity, memory, and fame. Pyramids appeared on gravestones, funeral monuments, and garden follies across Europe.

For the designers of the Great Seal, as Charles Thomson wrote, the pyramid signified "strength and duration." That is the essence of its symbolic meaning in the modern West. A pyramid says: this will last. It is built on a broad foundation. It is not going anywhere.

The unfinished pyramid

As we saw in Chapter Five, the pyramid on the Great Seal is unfinished. Its top is missing, and the eye floats in the space where the capstone should be. That image was meant to show a nation still under construction, with more work to do.

The unfinished pyramid has a powerful message for anyone starting something new. You do not have to finish the whole structure on the first day. You lay the foundation and then the first course of stones and then the next. Each step rests on the one below it. The top may be far away, but every layer brings you closer. A young business, like a young nation, is always an unfinished pyramid.

Steps and stairs

There is another way to look at a pyramid: as a staircase. The Step Pyramid of Djoser is literally a series of giant steps. Even the smooth-sided pyramids of Giza were built in layers, each a step up from the last. In many traditions, the pyramid or stepped tower represents a path upward, from the earth toward the heavens, from the material world toward the spiritual, from ignorance toward knowledge.

The ziggurats of Mesopotamia, great stepped temple towers with a shrine at the top, were imagined as places where heaven and earth met. The famous story of the Tower of Babel in the Book of Genesis is probably a memory of one of these towers, retold as a warning about human pride: the builders tried to reach heaven by their own power and ended in confusion.

So the pyramid carries a double lesson. It is a picture of ascent, of rising step by step toward something higher. But it is also a warning that the climb must be built on the right foundation and with the right motives. A tower built only to make a name for oneself may fall. A pyramid built on solid ground, with each stone set true, will stand.

The pyramid in business

In modern business and organizations, the pyramid has become a familiar way to picture structure. Organization charts show a few leaders at the top and many workers at the base. The famous "hierarchy of needs" proposed by the psychologist Abraham Maslow in the 1940s is usually drawn, by others who popularized it, as a pyramid, with basic physical needs at the bottom and self-fulfillment at the top. Food guides, sales funnels, and many other models use the same shape.

Not all of these uses are positive. The phrase "pyramid scheme" refers to a fraudulent business model in which early participants are paid with money from later recruits rather than from any real product or service, so that the scheme inevitably collapses when new recruits run out. Pyramid schemes are illegal in the United States and many other countries. It is worth saying clearly that the pyramid in the Conscientia emblem has nothing to do with such schemes. Meechie's World Inc sells real services and real products to real customers. The pyramid in our emblem is a symbol of strength and honest construction, not of recruitment.

Indeed, a true pyramid is the opposite of a pyramid scheme. In a real pyramid, every stone at the top is held up by solid stones below. Nothing is borrowed. Nothing is hollow. The structure is honest all the way down.

The pyramid and the triangle

When you look at a pyramid from the side, you see a triangle. This is why the eye in the triangle, the Eye of Providence, combines so naturally with the pyramid. The triangle that frames the eye in Christian art can be read as the top section of a pyramid, the capstone, seen from the front. On the Great Seal, the eye's triangle floats above the unfinished pyramid precisely as if it were its missing top. In the Conscientia emblem, the eye sits in a glowing capstone set just above the pyramid's top course, so close that the two read as one structure.

The next chapter looks more closely at the triangle as a shape: its geometry, its strength, and the many meanings it has carried. But before leaving the pyramid, it is worth summarizing what it brings to the emblem.

It stands for collective work. The pyramids were built by organized teams who took pride in their labor. Meechie's World Inc is a company that works with many people: clients, artists, members, partners. No one builds alone.

And it stands for ascent. Every step taken, every client served, every song released, every page built is one more course of stone, one step closer to the top.

At the very peak of the pyramid, where the Egyptians placed a golden capstone to catch the first light of dawn, our emblem places the eye. The highest point of the structure is not wealth or fame. It is conscience: the clear sight that keeps the whole structure honest.

The Triangle: Geometry of Strength

Let no one ignorant of geometry enter here.
inscription said to have stood over the door of Plato's Academy

A triangle is the simplest closed shape that can be drawn with straight lines. You cannot make a closed figure with one line or with two. With three, you can. That simplicity has made the triangle one of the most important shapes in mathematics, engineering, art, and symbolism. In the Conscientia emblem, the eye sits within a triangle that crowns a pyramid, like a capstone of light. This chapter explores why the triangle matters so much, and what it adds to the meaning of the emblem.

The strongest shape

Engineers have a simple test they like to show students. Take four sticks and join them at the corners to make a square. Push on one corner, and the square will easily collapse into a diamond shape, because the joints can rotate. Now take three sticks and join them into a triangle. Push on a corner, and nothing happens. The triangle holds its shape. It cannot be deformed without breaking one of its sides.

This is because, for any three given lengths, there is only one triangle that can be made from them. The shape is fixed by its sides. A square or rectangle, by contrast, can lean over into a parallelogram without any side changing length. This property makes the triangle the basic unit of strength in construction. Bridges, roof trusses, cranes, towers, bicycle frames, and the steel skeletons of skyscrapers are all built from triangles. The Eiffel Tower is a lattice of triangles. So are the great railroad bridges of the nineteenth century. When engineers want something light and strong, they reach for the triangle.

There is a lesson in this. Three points of support are stable in a way that two or four may not be. A three-legged stool will stand firm on uneven ground, while a four-legged chair will rock. A triangle is strong because every part supports every other part. Take away one side, and it falls apart. Keep all three, and it cannot be pushed out of shape.

Geometry and the ancient world

The ancient Egyptians used practical geometry to survey their fields after each flood of the Nile washed away the boundary markers, and to lay out their pyramids and temples with remarkable precision. The Greek historian Herodotus believed that geometry, whose name means "measuring the earth," was invented in Egypt for exactly this purpose.

The ancient Greeks turned geometry into a system of logical proof. The mathematician Euclid, working in Alexandria in Egypt around 300 BCE, wrote a book called the Elements, which built up the whole of geometry from a few basic definitions and assumptions. It became one of the most widely studied books in history, used as a textbook for more than two thousand years. The first proposition in the first book of Euclid's Elements shows how to construct an equilateral triangle, a triangle with three equal sides, using only a straightedge and compass.

One of the most famous results in all of mathematics concerns triangles: the theorem associated with Pythagoras, which states that in a right triangle, the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. Builders have used this fact for thousands of years to make right angles. A rope knotted into twelve equal sections can be stretched into a triangle with sides of three, four, and five units, and the angle between the shorter sides will be a perfect right angle. Whether or not the ancient Egyptians used this exact method, as is sometimes claimed, it is a simple and reliable technique that builders have used across many cultures.

For the Greeks, geometry was more than a practical tool. It was a path to truth. The philosopher Plato believed that the perfect forms of geometry, such as the ideal triangle that no drawing can perfectly reproduce, were more real than the imperfect objects of the physical world. A famous tradition holds that the entrance to Plato's school in Athens bore the inscription, "Let no one ignorant of geometry enter here." Whether or not the sign really existed, the idea it expresses was real: that clear, disciplined thinking begins with geometry.

The triangle as a sacred sign

Because of its simplicity, stability, and threefold nature, the triangle has been used as a sacred symbol in many traditions.

In Christian art, as we saw in Chapter Four, the equilateral triangle stands for the Trinity: one God in three persons, each equal to the others.

In Hindu and Buddhist tradition, triangles are central to the geometric diagrams called yantras and mandalas, used as aids to meditation. An upward-pointing triangle often stands for masculine energy, fire, or the god Shiva, while a downward-pointing triangle stands for feminine energy, water, or the goddess Shakti. The famous Sri Yantra is a complex arrangement of interlocking upward and downward triangles representing the union of these forces and the unfolding of the cosmos.

In the alchemy of medieval and Renaissance Europe, the four elements were represented by triangles: fire as an upward triangle, water as a downward triangle, air as an upward triangle with a horizontal line through it, and earth as a downward triangle with a line through it.

Two overlapping triangles, one pointing up and one pointing down, form a six-pointed star. This shape appears in many cultures. It is best known today as the Star of David, or Magen David, the symbol of Judaism and of the State of Israel, though its use as a specifically Jewish emblem became widespread only in the last few centuries. It also appears in Islamic art, where it is sometimes called the Seal of Solomon, and in Hindu temple design.

Three as a number of completeness

Part of the triangle's power comes from the number three itself. In many cultures, three is a number of completeness. There is a beginning, a middle, and an end. There is past, present, and future. There is mind, body, and spirit. Stories are often built in threes: three brothers, three wishes, three trials. Speeches and slogans are often built in threes, because the rhythm of three feels finished and memorable. Writers call this the rule of three.

The Conscientia emblem itself is built in threes. There are three central images: the eye, the pyramid, and the book. The full crest of the company carries three phrases: the company's name, the motto Lux e tenebris, and the motto Iustitiam quaerimus. The founder often describes the company's work in three broad areas: helping people with legal paperwork, creating music and media, and building digital tools and businesses. The triangle holds these threes together.

The pointing triangle

A triangle resting on its base points upward. It directs the eye toward its peak. This is one reason why triangles appear so often in sacred art and architecture: the steeple of a church, the spire of a cathedral, the minaret of a mosque, the peak of a pagoda, all draw the eye up toward the sky. An upward triangle suggests aspiration, growth, and ascent.

A triangle can also point forward, like an arrowhead or the prow of a ship. Road signs use triangles to warn and to direct. The "play" button on every music player and video app is a triangle pointing to the right, a small sign of motion forward in time.

In the Conscientia emblem, the triangle points upward. Its peak, the highest point of the emblem, is where the rays of light seem to originate. The eye sits just below that peak, as if looking down from the top of a mountain. The message is one of ascent toward clear sight.

The triangle and the eye

Why put an eye in a triangle at all, rather than in a circle or a square? The circle is the more natural frame for an eye, since an eye is round. But a circle has no direction; it is complete and closed. A square is stable but static. A triangle, by contrast, combines stability with direction. It sits firmly on its base while pointing upward. It is a frame that both holds the eye steady and lifts it up.

The triangle also gives the eye a sense of authority and focus. When an eye is set in a triangle, its gaze seems to come from a single point, like the vanishing point in a perspective drawing, where all lines meet. Renaissance artists discovered that, by arranging lines so that they converged on a single point, they could create a convincing illusion of depth. The triangle around the eye has a similar effect. It draws everything toward the center.

The triangle in Meechie's World

The triangle also has a special meaning within the culture of Meechie's World Inc. It is a shape of partnership. A triangle cannot stand with one side or two; it needs all three. In the same way, the company's work depends on three partners: the company itself, the client or member it serves, and the truth that both must honor. A legal document is only as good as the facts it rests on. A song is only as good as the honesty of the artist who records it. A website is only as good as the business it represents. When any one side is missing, the structure collapses.

The triangle is also a reminder of the strength of small, well-connected structures. A company does not need to be huge to be strong. A single triangle of steel, properly built, can carry an enormous load. A small company, built of well-joined parts, can do more than its size suggests.

The lesson of the strongest shape

The triangle teaches that strength comes not from size or decoration but from the right connections. Three sides, each supporting the others, make a shape that cannot be pushed out of true. In the Conscientia emblem, the triangle is the frame that holds the eye of conscience steady, the face of the pyramid that rises from the book, and the arrow that points from the darkness at the base toward the light at the peak.

With the pyramid and the triangle in place, we turn now to the foundation on which the whole emblem rests: the open book.

The Open Book

This chapter explores what the open book has meant across history, and why it forms the base of our emblem.

The miracle of writing

For most of human history, there was no writing. Knowledge was passed down by word of mouth, from parents to children, from elders to the young, from master to apprentice. Oral cultures developed remarkable feats of memory. Poets could recite thousands of lines. Genealogies could be traced back many generations. Laws and customs were held in the minds of the community.

But memory has limits. When the person who remembers dies, what they knew may die with them. Stories change in the retelling. Disputes arise about what was really said or agreed. Writing changed all of that. Writing allowed words to be fixed, preserved, and carried across distance and time. A written agreement could be checked. A written law could be read by anyone who knew the script. A written story could be read a thousand years later exactly as it was first set down.

Writing seems to have been invented independently in at least a few places: in Mesopotamia, where the Sumerians began pressing marks into clay tablets around 3300 to 3200 BCE; in Egypt, at about the same time; in China, by around 1200 BCE; and in Mesoamerica, by the first millennium BCE. In Mesopotamia, the earliest writing was used mostly for accounting: keeping track of grain, livestock, and labor. Writing began, in other words, as a way of keeping honest records. Poetry, law, history, and scripture came later.

From tablet to scroll to book

Early writing was done on clay tablets, stone, papyrus, wood, bamboo, bone, and animal skins. The Egyptians made a kind of paper from the papyrus reed and rolled long sheets of it into scrolls. The Greeks and Romans adopted the scroll. For centuries, a "book" meant a scroll.

The form of book we know today, with pages bound together along one edge, is called a codex. It became common in the Roman world in the first few centuries of the Common Era, and early Christians were among its most enthusiastic users. A codex had many advantages over a scroll. It was more compact. Both sides of each page could be written on. And, most importantly, a reader could open it to any page directly, instead of unrolling the whole scroll to find a passage. By the end of the ancient world, the codex had largely replaced the scroll.

The invention of printing transformed the book again. In China, woodblock printing was in use by the eighth century, and the oldest surviving dated printed book, a copy of the Buddhist Diamond Sutra, was printed in 868. Movable type made of ceramic was developed in China in the eleventh century, and metal movable type was used in Korea by the thirteenth century. In Europe, Johannes Gutenberg's development of a printing press with movable metal type in Mainz around 1450 led to an explosion of printed books. Within fifty years, millions of books had been printed across Europe. Knowledge that had been locked in a few handwritten manuscripts became available to anyone who could read.

The book as scripture

For billions of people, the most important book is a sacred one. Judaism, Christianity, and Islam are often called the religions of the Book, because each centers on a written revelation. The Torah, the Bible, and the Quran are not just collections of writings. For believers, they are the word of God, or the record of God's dealings with humanity, preserved in writing so that every generation can encounter it.

In Islam, the very first word revealed to the Prophet Muhammad, according to tradition, was a command: Iqra, meaning "Read" or "Recite." The opening verses of the ninety-sixth chapter of the Quran speak of God as the one who taught by the pen, who taught humanity what it did not know. The pen and the written word are honored as gifts of God. Islamic civilization developed some of the most beautiful calligraphy and some of the greatest libraries of the medieval world, including the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, where scholars translated and built upon the learning of Greece, Persia, and India.

In Judaism, the Torah scroll is treated with the greatest reverence. It is handwritten by trained scribes according to strict rules, kept in an ark in the synagogue, and read publicly throughout the year. When a Torah scroll becomes too worn to use, it is buried with honor.

In Christianity, the Gospel book is carried in procession, kissed, and incensed in many traditions. The Gospel of John begins with the famous words, "In the beginning was the Word." In many other traditions, too, sacred texts are central: the Vedas and Upanishads of Hinduism, the Pali Canon and the sutras of Buddhism, the Guru Granth Sahib of Sikhism, which is treated not just as a book but as the living Guru.

Light as knowledge

Because we see by light, light became the universal symbol of knowledge and understanding. Plato, in his famous Allegory of the Cave, imagined human beings as prisoners chained in a dark cave, watching shadows on the wall and mistaking them for reality. The philosopher is the one who breaks free, climbs out of the cave, and sees the world in the light of the sun. At first the light is painful; his eyes are dazzled. But gradually he learns to see things as they really are. When he goes back into the cave to tell the others, they do not believe him.

Plato's allegory has been retold and reinterpreted for more than two thousand years. It is the story of every person who has had to learn something difficult, who has struggled out of confusion into understanding, and who has then faced the challenge of explaining it to people who are still in the dark. It is a story that anyone who has ever represented themselves in a courtroom, or tried to make sense of a complicated legal system, will recognize. The first encounter with the law can feel like being blinded. But with study and help, the shapes come into focus.

The European intellectual movement of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries took its very name from this imagery. In English it is called the Enlightenment. In French it was les Lumières, "the lights." In German, Aufklärung, "clearing up." The thinkers of the Enlightenment believed that reason, science, and education could bring humanity out of the darkness of ignorance, superstition, and tyranny into the light of knowledge and freedom.

Light in the faiths

In nearly every religious tradition, light is a central image of the divine.

In the Christian Gospel of John, Jesus says, "I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." The prologue of the same Gospel speaks of a light that shines in the darkness, which the darkness has not overcome.

In the Quran, one of the most celebrated passages is the Verse of Light, in the twenty-fourth chapter, which begins: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." It goes on to describe this light with the image of a niche in which there is a lamp, the lamp enclosed in glass, the glass shining like a brilliant star, lit from a blessed olive tree whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it: light upon light. Elsewhere, the Quran describes God as the protector of those who believe, who brings them out of the darknesses into the light. The Arabic phrase, mina al-zulumati ila al-nur, from the darknesses into the light, is very close in meaning to our motto, Lux e tenebris.

In Judaism, light is honored in the lighting of candles to welcome the Sabbath, and in the festival of Hanukkah, which remembers the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem and the miracle of a small supply of oil that burned for eight days. In Hinduism, the great festival of Diwali, the festival of lights, celebrates the victory of light over darkness and good over evil, and homes are lit with rows of small oil lamps. In Buddhism, enlightenment, bodhi, is the awakening from the darkness of ignorance. In Zoroastrianism, one of the oldest living religions, fire and light represent truth and the god Ahura Mazda.

Across these very different traditions, the same pattern holds. Light stands for what is true, good, and holy. Darkness stands for what is false, evil, or not yet redeemed. And the movement from darkness to light is the movement of salvation, of learning, of awakening.

The history of the motto

The Latin phrase lux e tenebris, light out of darkness, is a short and natural Latin expression, and variations of it have been used as mottos by many families, schools, and organizations over the centuries. A close relative is the phrase post tenebras lux, "after darkness, light," which became the motto of the city of Geneva during the Protestant Reformation of the sixteenth century. It is drawn from the Latin translation of the Book of Job, where Job, in the depths of his suffering, speaks of hoping for light after darkness. The phrase is carved on the Reformation Wall in Geneva, a monument to the leaders of the Protestant Reformation.

Lux e tenebris has a slightly different emphasis. Post tenebras lux describes a sequence in time: first darkness, then light. Lux e tenebris describes a source: light comes out of darkness. It is not just that light follows darkness, but that light is drawn from it, born from it, brought up out of it. The darkness is not simply replaced; it is transformed.

This distinction matters for the meaning of the motto in the Conscientia emblem. Meechie's World Inc does not pretend that darkness does not exist. Many of the people the company serves are facing hard circumstances: legal trouble, incarceration of a loved one, financial struggle, or simply the frustration of trying to be heard in a world that does not seem to listen. The motto does not say that these things are not real. It says that light can come out of them. A hard experience can become a source of wisdom. A courtroom battle can become a lesson in justice. A painful life can become a powerful song.

Out of the dark

There is a long tradition of art, music, and literature born from struggle. Many of the most powerful songs in American history came out of suffering: the spirituals sung by enslaved people, the blues of the Mississippi Delta, the protest songs of the civil rights movement, and the rap and hip-hop that came out of neighborhoods neglected by those in power. In each case, people took the darkness of their circumstances and made something luminous out of it. They told the truth about their lives, and the truth became art.

Hip-hop, in particular, began in the 1970s in the Bronx, New York, at a time when the borough was suffering from poverty, arson, and abandonment by public institutions. Young people with very little money built a culture out of turntables, spray paint, dance, and words. That culture became one of the most influential art forms in the world. It is a vivid example of light out of darkness.

Meechie's World Inc is, among other things, a music company. Its radio station, its recording and production services, and its support for artists all flow from the conviction that the voices of people who have been through the dark deserve to be heard. The founder's own music, recorded over many years, belongs to this tradition. Lux e tenebris is not an abstract slogan. It is a description of how art and hope are made.

The rays of the emblem

In the Conscientia emblem, the light takes the form of rays streaming outward from the eye at the peak of the pyramid. These rays are descendants of the glory that surrounds the Eye of Providence in Christian art, and of the solar rays of ancient sun gods. But in our emblem they have a specific meaning. They show that the eye of conscience is not only receiving light, seeing what is there, but also giving light, illuminating what is around it.

This is an important point about conscience. A conscience that only watches and judges can become harsh and fearful. A conscience that gives light helps us see the way forward. It does not just tell us when we have done wrong. It shows us how to do right. In the same way, the work of Meechie's World Inc is meant to shed light: to explain, to clarify, to make visible what was hidden and understandable what was confusing.

Darkness as the beginning

There is one more thing to say about darkness. In the emblem, the background is black. The gold of the eye, the pyramid, the book, and the rays shines out against it. Without the darkness, the light would not be visible. A candle in daylight is hardly noticed. A candle in a dark room is everything.

The founder of Meechie's World Inc chose black as the field of the emblem deliberately. Black represents where we start, the difficulty and obscurity from which every effort begins. It also represents strength, seriousness, and depth. And it is a reminder that the light we bring matters most in the darkest places. A company that only served people whose lives were already easy would not need a motto like Lux e tenebris. A company that seeks to serve those who are struggling needs it every day.

Living the motto

What does it mean, in practice, to live by the motto Lux e tenebris? For Meechie's World Inc, it means several things.

It means explaining things clearly. Legal procedures, business requirements, technical systems: these are often wrapped in jargon and complexity that keeps ordinary people in the dark. The company's job is to turn the light on.

It means telling the truth. Darkness is where lies hide. A company that wants to be a source of light must be honest with its clients, its members, and the public about what it can and cannot do.

It means turning struggle into strength. Every hard experience a client brings can become the foundation of a better future: a case documented, a song recorded, a business launched.

And it means keeping the lamp lit for others. Light that is hoarded is wasted. The point of carrying a light through the darkness is so that others can see the way, too.

Chapter Twelve

Conscientia: The Word Beneath

My conscience means more to me than what all the world says.
Cicero, Letters to Atticus

Every element of the emblem we have discussed so far, the eye, the pyramid, the triangle, the book, the light, is an image. But beneath the images, holding them together, is a word. CONSCIENTIA. It is the name of the emblem and the key to its meaning. This chapter explores where the word comes from, what it has meant to philosophers, theologians, and ordinary people across two thousand years, and why it was chosen as the word that defines the house of Meechie's World.

Knowing together

Conscientia is a Latin word. It is formed from two parts: the prefix con-, meaning "with" or "together," and scientia, meaning "knowledge." Scientia is the source of our word science. So conscientia means, literally, "knowing with" or "knowledge shared with."

But knowledge shared with whom? In its earliest uses in Latin, conscientia could mean simply a shared knowledge between people: being in on a secret, being aware of something along with others, being an accomplice or a witness. If two people knew about a crime, they had conscientia of it. The word could describe the knowledge that a group held in common.

Gradually, the word turned inward. Conscientia came to mean the knowledge one shares with oneself: the awareness of one's own thoughts and deeds, and especially the moral awareness of whether those deeds were right or wrong. You are the witness to your own life. You know what you have done, even if no one else does. That inner witness is conscience.

The Roman orator and philosopher Marcus Tullius Cicero, writing in the first century BCE, used the word in this moral sense. In one of his letters to his friend Atticus, he wrote that his own conscience meant more to him than all the talk of the world. Whatever people might say about him, he knew in himself whether he had acted rightly, and that inner knowledge was what mattered.

The Greek background

The Latin word conscientia had a Greek counterpart, syneidesis, which is built in exactly the same way: syn, meaning "with," and eidesis, from a root meaning "to know" or "to see." Remarkably, this Greek word is related to the same root that gives us the words "idea" and "video," and that connects knowing with seeing. The ancient languages themselves knew that conscience is a kind of inner sight. The eye in our emblem is not a random choice. It is written into the history of the word.

The apostle Paul, writing in Greek in the first century, uses syneidesis many times in his letters. In his Letter to the Romans, he says that even people who do not have the written law of Moses show that the requirements of the law are written on their hearts, their consciences also bearing witness, their thoughts accusing or excusing them. For Paul, conscience is a universal human capacity, an inner law that everyone has, whether or not they have read the scriptures. When the New Testament was translated into Latin, syneidesis became conscientia.

Conscience in the Middle Ages

Medieval philosophers and theologians thought hard about conscience. The great thirteenth-century Italian theologian Thomas Aquinas made an important distinction. On the one hand, there is a basic, built-in awareness of the most fundamental moral principles, such as "do good and avoid evil." Medieval thinkers gave this a special name, synderesis. It cannot be lost, and it never errs. On the other hand, there is conscientia, which is the act of applying those principles to particular situations: judging that this action, here and now, is right or wrong. Conscientia, for Aquinas, can make mistakes, because we can misunderstand the situation or reason badly. But we are still bound to follow it, because it is our best judgment of what is right.

This distinction is useful even today. It tells us that conscience is not just a feeling. It is a judgment, a work of the mind. It requires knowledge of the facts and careful thought. A good conscience is an informed conscience. This is why, in the Conscientia emblem, the eye rests on the open book. Conscience needs knowledge to work well.

Conscience and freedom

In the centuries that followed, conscience became one of the great battlegrounds of human freedom. In 1521, the German reformer Martin Luther was summoned before the Holy Roman Emperor at the Diet of Worms and ordered to take back his writings. He refused, declaring, according to the traditional account, that his conscience was captive to the Word of God, and that to go against conscience was neither right nor safe. Whatever one thinks of Luther's theology, his stand became a symbol of the individual conscience standing against power.

Over the following centuries, the idea of freedom of conscience became one of the foundations of modern rights. The First Amendment to the United States Constitution, which protects the free exercise of religion and freedom of speech, grew out of long struggles for the right of each person to follow conscience in matters of faith. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the United Nations in 1948, begins its first article by declaring that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights, and that they are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood.

Conscience is not only a private matter. It has shaped history. Abolitionists who fought slavery appealed to the conscience of the nation. Civil rights activists who sat at segregated lunch counters and marched across bridges appealed to conscience. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., in his Letter from Birmingham Jail in 1963, argued that an individual who breaks a law that conscience tells him is unjust, and who willingly accepts the penalty in order to arouse the conscience of the community, is in reality expressing the highest respect for law. Conscience, in this sense, is the force that pushes laws to become more just.

Conscience and consciousness

In English, the words conscience and consciousness both come from the Latin conscientia. For a long time, the two meanings were not clearly separated. To be conscious of something was to know it, to be aware of it. To have a conscience was to know right from wrong. Only gradually did English split the one Latin word into two. In French, the single word conscience still covers both meanings: awareness and moral sense.

This shared root is a reminder that conscience is a form of awareness. A person with no awareness of what they are doing cannot have a conscience about it. Moral life begins with paying attention: to what we are doing, to its effects on others, to the truth of the situation. The eye in the emblem is, among other things, the eye of attention.

Why Conscientia?

When the founder of Meechie's World Inc chose a single word to sit beneath the eye and the pyramid, he could have chosen many. He could have chosen a word for power, wealth, or success. He chose conscience. Why?

The first reason is that it names what the eye means. Without a word beneath it, the eye in the pyramid is open to every interpretation, including the fearful ones discussed in Chapter Seven. With the word Conscientia beneath it, the meaning is fixed. This is not the eye of a secret society. It is the eye of conscience: the awareness that sees our actions and judges them honestly.

The second reason is that it names the standard of the company. A company that prepares legal documents, handles payments, publishes books, records music, and builds websites for other people is trusted with a great deal. Its clients often cannot check everything it does. They have to trust that the work is honest. Conscientia says: we will do the work as if someone is always watching, because someone is. We are watching ourselves.

The third reason is the meaning of "knowing together." Meechie's World Inc is a community as well as a company. Its website brings together members, artists, clients, and friends. Its radio station is built so that everyone hears the same song at the same moment. Its legal work is a collaboration between the client, who knows the facts, and the preparer, who knows the forms and the procedures. Knowledge shared is knowledge multiplied. Conscientia is the knowledge we hold in common.

The fourth reason is personal. The founder has said that he wants his inventions and ideas to live on, and that the company is meant to outlast him. A company built on conscience has a chance to do that, because conscience is what keeps an institution honest when the founder is no longer in the room. A rule written in a handbook can be ignored. A culture of conscience is harder to lose.

A conscience that can be trusted

It is easy to put a fine word on a logo. It is harder to live up to it. Many companies have mission statements full of noble words that bear little relation to how they actually behave. The word Conscientia is meant to be a standing challenge to Meechie's World Inc, not a decoration. Every time it appears at the top of a document, the company is asking itself: does this work deserve this word?

A conscience that can be trusted has several qualities. It is informed: it knows the facts and the rules. It is honest: it does not lie to itself about what it has done. It is consistent: it applies the same standards in private as in public. It is humble: it knows it can make mistakes, and it is willing to correct them. And it is courageous: it is willing to say no when no is the right answer, even when yes would be easier or more profitable.

These qualities will be set out more fully in Chapter Twenty-Four, which describes the code of conduct of the house. For now, it is enough to say that the word beneath the emblem is the foundation of everything else. The eye sees. The pyramid stands. The book records. The light shines. But it is conscience that holds them together.

Iustitiam quaerimus

Conscience naturally leads to justice. A person who knows right from wrong cannot rest content when wrong is being done. The second motto of the house, Iustitiam quaerimus, we seek justice, grows directly out of the word Conscientia. Before we turn to that motto, however, Part Three will put the pieces of the emblem together and examine it as a whole.

Reading the Emblem

Chapter Thirteen

Anatomy of the Conscientia Emblem

Every part of a true sign speaks; nothing is there by accident.
house saying of Meechie's World Inc

We have now followed each element of the emblem through its long history. It is time to put them together and look at the Conscientia emblem itself, piece by piece, the way a student of heraldry reads a coat of arms or an art historian reads a painting. This chapter is a guided tour of the emblem from the bottom up. By the end of it, you should be able to look at the emblem and read it like a sentence.

The field

Every emblem has a background, which in heraldry is called the field. The field of the Conscientia emblem is black, a deep, warm black with a faint glow of gold around the eye. The black is not empty. It is the darkness out of which the light comes, the tenebrae of the motto Lux e tenebris. Everything else in the emblem is drawn in gold against it, so that the eye of the viewer reads the emblem the way a traveler sees a lit window at night.

The open book

At the base of the emblem lies an open book. It is wide, spreading almost the full width of the emblem, and it is drawn with its two pages curving gently upward from the spine, as a real book does when it lies open on a table. On each page there are lines suggesting text: four lines on the left page and four on the right, drawn as gentle curves that follow the curve of the paper. The pages are framed in gold, and the edges of more pages can be seen stacked beneath the open spread, showing that this is a thick book, with much more to read.

From the center of the book, at the spine, hangs a small red ribbon bookmark. It is the only red in the emblem. That small mark of color is easy to miss, but it carries meaning. A bookmark marks a place: the page where the reader stopped, the passage that matters, the point to return to. In the emblem it says that this book is being read, that someone is working through it, page by page, and has marked where they are. The red also recalls the red seals and ribbons once used to bind official legal documents, the origin of the phrase "red tape." In a company that prepares legal papers, a red ribbon on an open book is a quiet nod to the paperwork of justice.

The book is the foundation. Everything else in the emblem rests on it.

The pyramid

Standing on the open book is a pyramid. It is drawn as a pyramid seen from the front, so that it appears as a broad shape with a flat base and sides sloping inward toward the top. But it is not a complete pyramid. Its top is cut off flat, so that its outline is a trapezoid, wide at the bottom and narrower at the top. This is a truncated pyramid, the same kind of unfinished pyramid that appears on the Great Seal of the United States.

The pyramid is built of stone blocks laid in courses, the horizontal layers in which masons lay stone. There are four courses, each with its blocks offset from the course below, as real masonry is laid so that the joints do not line up and the wall is strong. The blocks are outlined in gold.

The face of the pyramid is divided by light. The left side glows faintly warmer, as if lit by the rays from above, and the right side is darker, in shadow. This division of light and shadow gives the pyramid depth and shows the direction of the light. It also carries the motto of the house in visual form: one side of the structure is in the light, the other is still in darkness, and the light is moving across it.

Along the upper left edge of the pyramid runs a thin line of highlight, like a gleam on polished stone. Across the top course runs another thin line of highlight. These small touches make the pyramid look solid and real, not flat.

The capstone and the eye

Above the pyramid, separated from it by a narrow gap, is the capstone: a small triangle that completes the shape of the pyramid. If you imagine the gap closed, the capstone would sit exactly on the top course and finish the pyramid.

The capstone is drawn in gold with a double outline, an outer triangle and a thinner inner triangle, and its interior is dark. Within it is the eye. The eye is drawn as an almond-shaped outline in gold, with a round gold iris and a dark pupil. There is a small white highlight in the pupil, the gleam of light that makes an eye look alive. Above the eye, a single curved line suggests an eyebrow or the arch of the upper lid.

The capstone glows. Behind it, a soft halo of golden light radiates into the black field, so that the capstone seems to float in its own light.

Why is the capstone separated from the pyramid by a gap? On the Great Seal, the gap expresses the unfinished state of the nation, with the completion of the work left to providence. In the Conscientia emblem, the gap is narrow, almost closed. It says that the work is nearly complete, that the crown is within reach, but that it is a different kind of thing from the stones below. The stones of the pyramid are the work: the documents, the songs, the websites, the clients served. The capstone is the conscience that crowns the work and gives it meaning. You cannot build conscience out of stone. It has to be added from above, as a gift of light. But it belongs on top of the work, and it fits it exactly.

The rays

From the capstone, rays of light stream outward in a fan across the upper half of the emblem. There are thirteen rays in all: one standing straight up from the peak, and six on each side, alternating between long, bold rays and shorter, finer ones. The longest rays reach out horizontally to each side, at the level of the eye.

The number thirteen is not an accident. It echoes the thirteen steps of the pyramid on the Great Seal, the thirteen stars, stripes, arrows, and olive leaves of the American seal, and the thirteen original states. But in the Conscientia emblem it has an additional meaning. Thirteen is a number that many people consider unlucky. By using it for the rays of light, the emblem turns a number of bad luck into a number of illumination. It is light out of darkness, even in its numbers.

The alternation of long and short rays gives the light a sense of shimmer and movement, the way real light seems to pulse when you look at a bright source. It also creates a rhythm: strong, gentle, strong, gentle, like a heartbeat or a drum.

The stars and points of light

Scattered in the black field around the pyramid are small points of light. To the left and right of the capstone, at the level of the rays, are two four-pointed stars, drawn in a pale gold. Below them, at the sides of the pyramid, are small round dots of light, like distant stars or sparks.

The stars place the emblem in the night sky. They show that the darkness of the field is not empty but full of light, if one looks for it. The two larger stars, one on each side, also create a balance and symmetry around the central axis of the emblem.

The axis

The whole emblem is built around a vertical line running down its center. The central ray, the peak of the capstone, the eye, the center of the pyramid, the spine of the book, and the red bookmark all line up along this axis. This gives the emblem a sense of order, balance, and uprightness. It stands straight. In the old language of the builders, it is plumb.

An upright axis is a symbol of integrity. The word integrity comes from the Latin integer, meaning whole or undivided. A person of integrity is the same through and through, from top to bottom, without hidden contradictions. The central axis of the emblem runs unbroken from the light at the top to the book at the bottom. It says that conscience and knowledge are connected in a single straight line.

Reading the emblem as a sentence

Now we can read the whole emblem from bottom to top, like a sentence.

At the bottom is the open book: knowledge, law, and the written record, open for anyone to read, with a mark showing where the reader is in the work.

On the book stands the pyramid: a structure of strength and endurance, built stone by stone in courses, by honest labor, partly in light and partly still in shadow.

Above the pyramid, completing it, is the capstone of conscience, in which the eye of awareness looks out, clear and alive.

From the eye, light streams out in thirteen rays, illuminating the darkness around it, turning a number of bad luck into a number of light.

Around it all, the night is full of stars.

Put into words: On a foundation of open knowledge, we build a strong and lasting work, stone by stone, and we crown it with conscience, which sees clearly and gives light to the darkness around it.

That is the Conscientia emblem.

The emblem and the word

In many of its uses, the emblem appears with the word CONSCIENTIA set beneath it or beside it, often in the form MEECHIE'S WORLD INC • CONSCIENTIA. On the documents prepared by the company, the emblem appears centered at the top of each page, with this line in small capitals beneath it and a thin gold rule below. The word names the emblem, and the emblem illustrates the word. Neither is complete without the other.

A modern emblem with ancient roots

It is worth noticing what kind of drawing the emblem is. It is not a medieval woodcut, a baroque engraving, or an Egyptian relief. It is a clean, modern line drawing, with bold gold strokes, rounded corners, and subtle gradients of light. It is designed to look good on a phone screen as well as on a printed page, on a T-shirt as well as on a legal document. It belongs to the twenty-first century.

Yet every element in it has roots that go back thousands of years: the eye to the temples of Mesopotamia and Egypt, the pyramid to Giza, the triangle to Euclid and the theologians of the Trinity, the book to the first scribes and the religions of the Book, the light to the opening lines of Genesis and the Verse of Light. The emblem is a new branch on a very old tree.
