Chapter Twenty-Six

The Eye in Popular Culture

Art is a lie that makes us realize truth.
Pablo Picasso

The chapters of Part One followed the eye from the ancient world to the founding of the United States and the lodges of the Freemasons. But the story did not end there. In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, the eye in the triangle escaped from churches, seals, and lodges into the wider world of popular culture: novels, films, album covers, fashion, video games, and the endless scroll of social media. This companion chapter looks at how the eye lives in popular culture today, and especially in the music culture that Meechie's World Inc belongs to.

The eye as a mood

In popular culture, the eye in the triangle is rarely used for its original meaning. Few designers who put it on a T-shirt are thinking about providence or the Trinity. Instead, the eye has become a kind of mood: a way of signaling mystery, power, secret knowledge, or rebellion. It looks ancient and esoteric. It hints at hidden meanings. It is, to put it simply, cool.

This is not new. Artists and designers have always borrowed symbols for their emotional effect. The skull has gone from a Christian reminder of death, memento mori, to a pirate flag to a fashion print. The cross has gone from an instrument of execution to a sacred sign to a piece of jewelry. Symbols that carry strong feelings are bound to be borrowed.

The danger, as Chapter Seven explained, is that borrowed symbols can lose their history and pick up new, distorted meanings. The eye has been borrowed so often for its air of mystery that many people now assume mystery is all it means.

Novels and films

The eye and the pyramid have appeared in many popular novels and films. Thrillers about secret societies, hidden treasures, and codes have made the Great Seal, the Freemasons, and the Illuminati familiar to millions of readers who have never studied any of them. Some of these stories are carefully researched; many mix real history with invention in ways that readers may not be able to separate. A novel is free to imagine, of course. That is what novels are for. But the popularity of such stories has helped shape a public image of the eye as a sign of conspiracy.

In fantasy fiction and film, the image of a great, lidless, watching eye has become one of the most powerful pictures of evil: a dark lord who sees everything and controls everything through surveillance and fear. This is the reverse of the Eye of Providence. Where the Eye of Providence watches in order to care and protect, the evil eye of fantasy watches in order to dominate. Both images draw on the same deep human feeling about being seen; they simply point it in opposite directions.

The difference between these two eyes is the difference the word Conscientia is meant to mark. An eye that watches with conscience protects. An eye that watches without conscience controls.

Album covers and hip-hop

In music, the eye, the pyramid, and Egyptian imagery have long been popular on album covers, stage designs, and music videos. Funk and soul artists of the 1970s, notably George Clinton's Parliament-Funkadelic, along with Earth, Wind and Fire, drew on Egyptian and cosmic imagery, pyramids and eyes included, as part of a celebration of African heritage and Afrofuturist imagination. For many Black artists, ancient Egypt has been a source of pride: a great African civilization that built the pyramids long before Europe built its cathedrals.

In hip-hop, Egyptian imagery and esoteric symbols have been used in many ways. Some artists drew on teachings associated with groups such as the Nation of Islam and the Nation of Gods and Earths, sometimes called the Five Percenters, whose language and ideas influenced a generation of rappers in the 1980s and 1990s, and which used ideas of hidden knowledge and self-knowledge as paths to empowerment. Others used the pyramid and the eye simply as symbols of wealth, power, and success: reaching the top of the pyramid.

In the 2000s and 2010s, as described in Chapter Seven, internet rumors began to accuse major rappers and pop stars of being members of the Illuminati, pointing to hand gestures, album art, and lyrics as evidence. Some artists responded by mocking the rumors. Others leaned into them for publicity, deliberately using eyes and triangles to provoke speculation, because controversy sells records. The result has been a strange loop: the more people believed the rumors, the more artists used the symbols, and the more artists used the symbols, the more people believed the rumors.

Why artists use the eye

It is worth thinking about why artists, and especially artists from marginalized communities, are drawn to symbols of hidden power and secret knowledge. For people who have been shut out of official institutions, the idea of a knowledge that the powerful do not want you to have can be very appealing. It suggests that the system is not as solid as it looks, that there are other ways to the top, and that the truth is being kept from you.

There is a real insight in that feeling. Knowledge has often been deliberately kept from oppressed people. In much of the American South before the Civil War, it was illegal to teach enslaved people to read. For generations after slavery, Black schools were systematically underfunded. Legal systems have been made confusing and inaccessible in ways that disadvantage people without money. The feeling that knowledge is being hidden is not paranoid. It has historical foundations.

The difference between the conspiracy theory and the truth is in where the hidden knowledge actually lies. It is not in a secret society's coded symbols. It is in libraries, law books, court records, and schools that were unequally distributed. The most radical response to hidden knowledge is not to decode album covers. It is to open the book.

That is why the book in the Conscientia emblem is open, and why it sits at the foundation. Meechie's World Inc borrows the eye and the pyramid from popular culture as well as from history, but it adds the open book and the word Conscientia to say: the knowledge is not secret. It is right here. Come and read.

Fashion and streetwear

In fashion and streetwear, the eye in the triangle appears on shirts, hats, jewelry, and sneakers. It is often paired with gold, black, and Egyptian motifs, much like the Conscientia emblem. For many wearers, it is simply a striking design. For some, it is a statement of spirituality, ambition, or rebellion. For others, it is an ironic nod to conspiracy culture.

The clothing of Meechie's World Inc uses the eye with a specific meaning. A shirt bearing the Conscientia emblem is not a joke about the Illuminati and not a vague gesture toward mystery. It carries a named emblem with a written meaning. Anyone who asks the wearer what it means can be told: it is the eye of conscience, over the book of knowledge, with the mottos light out of darkness and we seek justice. That is a conversation worth having.

Social media and the endless eye

Social media itself has become a kind of all-seeing eye. Every post can be seen, shared, and saved. People curate their lives for an imagined audience that is always watching. The feeling of being watched, which the earliest eye symbols tried to capture, has become a constant condition of modern life.

This has effects that the ancient makers of eye charms would have recognized. Being constantly seen can make people more careful, more performative, and more anxious. It can also, as the experiments with pictures of eyes suggested, make people more conscious of how their behavior looks to others.

The question the emblem asks in this setting is whether we can turn the outer eye of social media into an inner eye of conscience. It is easy to behave well when the camera is on. The harder and more important thing is to be the same person when it is off.

The eye reclaimed

Popular culture has taken the eye in many directions: mystery, menace, glamour, rebellion, irony. Meechie's World Inc does not reject popular culture. It is a music company, a media company, a fashion company. It lives in that world. But it uses the eye deliberately, with its meaning written beneath it.

In a culture where symbols are borrowed and emptied of meaning every day, there is something powerful about a symbol that comes with an explanation. This book is that explanation. When people see the Conscientia emblem in a video, on a shirt, or on a website, and wonder what it means, the answer does not have to be a rumor. It can be a reading.

Chapter Twenty-Seven

The Numbers of the Emblem

Number rules the universe.
a saying attributed to the Pythagoreans

Numbers have always been symbols as well as tools. The ancient Pythagoreans believed that the whole cosmos was built on numerical harmony. Medieval cathedral builders designed their churches with symbolic proportions. Religious texts are full of meaningful numbers: seven days of creation, twelve tribes, forty days in the wilderness, ninety-nine names of God. The Conscientia emblem, too, is built with numbers in mind. This companion chapter looks at the numbers in the emblem and the crest, and at what they have meant across history.

One

There is one eye. One axis runs through the center of the emblem. One word, Conscientia, names it.

One is the number of unity and of beginning. In mathematics, it is the first counting number, the unit from which all others are made. In many religious traditions, it is the number of God. The central confession of Judaism, the Shema, declares that the Lord is one. The central confession of Islam, the shahada, begins by declaring that there is no god but God, and the doctrine of tawhid, the oneness of God, is the foundation of Islamic theology. In Christianity, despite the doctrine of the Trinity, God is confessed as one God.

In the emblem, the single eye stands for the unity of conscience. A person has one conscience, not one for business and another for home, not one for public and another for private. The single eye says: be the same everywhere.

The Gospel of Matthew contains a saying, quoted in Chapter One, about the eye as the lamp of the body. In older English translations, Jesus says that if your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light. A "single" eye, in that old sense, meant one that was clear, sound, and undivided. That is exactly the eye of conscience.

Two

There are two stars, one on each side of the rays. There are two pages in the open book. There are two mottos in the crest. There are two colors, gold and black.

Two is the number of balance and of pairs: left and right, light and dark, day and night, question and answer. It is also the number of dialogue and of relationship. It takes two to make an agreement, two to have a conversation, two sides to make a case.

In the emblem, the twos express balance. The two stars balance each other across the central axis. The two pages of the book show that knowledge has two sides, as every case has two sides, and that both must be read. The two mottos describe two movements: bringing light out, and seeking justice. The two colors express the contrast between darkness and light.

Three

There are three main elements in the emblem: the eye, the pyramid, and the book. The capstone is a triangle with three sides. The crest has three bands of text: the name, the first motto, and the second motto.

As Chapter Nine explained, three is the number of the triangle, the strongest shape, and of completeness: beginning, middle, and end. In Christian tradition, it is the number of the Trinity. In many folk traditions, things happen in threes. In rhetoric, the rule of three makes a phrase memorable.

In the emblem, the three main elements form a complete statement: knowledge, structure, and conscience. Remove any one of them, and the meaning collapses, just as a triangle falls apart when one side is removed.

Four

The pyramid of the emblem has four courses of stone. The open book has four lines of text on each page. The Great Pyramid, like all true pyramids, has four sides, oriented, in the case of the Giza pyramids, very closely to the four cardinal directions: north, south, east, and west.

Four is the number of the earth and of stability. There are four directions, four seasons, and, in the old science, four elements. A square has four sides and four right angles; it is the shape of foundations, of rooms, of city blocks. In many traditions, four represents the material world, as three represents the spiritual.

In the emblem, the four courses of the pyramid rest on the four lines of the book's pages. The structure of the work, its foundation in the material world, rests on knowledge. Four courses also suggest that the work has progressed through several stages and is solidly established, but is not yet finished.

Seven

The number seven does not appear directly in the emblem, but it appears in its background. In the Book of Zechariah, discussed in Chapter Three, the eyes of the Lord are seven, ranging through the whole earth. Seven is the number of days in the week, of the classical planets visible to the naked eye, of the notes in a musical scale, of the colors traditionally counted in the rainbow. In many traditions it is the number of perfection and completion. In Islam, the heavens are described as seven, and pilgrims circle the Kaaba seven times.

In the life of a company, seven is a good reminder of rest. The week has seven days, and in the Jewish and Christian scriptures, the seventh is a day of rest. No pyramid was ever built by workers who never rested. A sustainable house builds rest into its rhythm.

Nine

There are nine laurel leaves on each side of the wreath in the crest. Nine is three times three, the triangle multiplied by itself. In Greek mythology, there were nine Muses, the goddesses of the arts and sciences: epic poetry, history, love poetry, music, tragedy, sacred song, dance, comedy, and astronomy. A laurel wreath of nine leaves on each side is a fitting crown for a house devoted to the arts.

The founder has said that the company has completed legal document work for nine clients. The number is a coincidence, of course, but it is a pleasing one: each of those clients is, in a sense, a leaf in the wreath.

Thirteen

The most important number in the emblem is thirteen, the number of the rays of light.

As Chapter Five explained, thirteen is the number of the original American states, and it appears again and again on the Great Seal: thirteen steps of the pyramid, thirteen stars, thirteen stripes, thirteen arrows, thirteen olive leaves, and thirteen letters in the motto E Pluribus Unum, as well as in Annuit Coeptis.

But thirteen is better known as an unlucky number. Fear of the number thirteen even has a name: triskaidekaphobia. Many buildings skip the thirteenth floor. Friday the thirteenth is considered unlucky in many Western countries. The reasons for this superstition are debated. Some connect it to the Last Supper, at which there were thirteen at the table, the thirteenth being, in some tellings, Judas. Others connect it to Norse mythology, in which the trickster god Loki arrives as the uninvited thirteenth guest at a banquet. Others suggest it simply comes from thirteen following twelve, a number of completeness in many systems, so that thirteen seems to spill over and disrupt the order.

In other traditions, thirteen is not unlucky at all. In Judaism, the age of thirteen is the age of bar mitzvah, when a boy becomes responsible for keeping the commandments, and Jewish tradition counts thirteen attributes of God's mercy. In the Maya calendar, thirteen was an important sacred number.

The Conscientia emblem uses thirteen rays deliberately, as an act of transformation. It takes a number many people fear and makes it the number of light. This is Lux e tenebris in numerical form. It says that nothing is inherently unlucky, that what others see as a bad omen can become a source of illumination. For a company that works with people who have been told their situation is hopeless, this is a meaningful message.

Numbers without superstition

It should be said clearly that this chapter is about symbolism, not superstition. The numbers in the emblem were chosen and arranged for their meanings and for their visual balance. They do not have magical powers. Thirteen rays will not bring good luck, and four courses of stone will not guarantee stability. What brings good fortune to a business is good work, honestly done. What brings stability is a solid foundation of knowledge and conscience.

But symbols matter because they remind us. A number on an emblem can remind us of a lesson, just as a knot in a handkerchief reminds us of an errand. One eye: be the same everywhere. Two pages: read both sides. Three elements: knowledge, structure, conscience. Four courses: build on the book. Nine leaves: honor the arts. Thirteen rays: turn bad luck into light.

Counting the house

There is one more number worth considering: the number of people the house serves. Every company, in the end, is measured not by the symbolism of its emblem but by the lives it touches. That number starts small. One client. Nine clients. A few hundred members. A few thousand listeners. But every great house started with a small count.

The Great Seal of the United States was designed for a nation of thirteen states and a few million people. Today the nation has fifty states and hundreds of millions of people, and the seal still bears the number thirteen, a reminder of where it began. Whatever Meechie's World Inc grows into, its thirteen rays will remember where the light first came from.

Chapter Twenty-Eight

Seals, Signatures and the Maker's Mark

By their fruits you shall know them.
Matthew 7:20

The Conscientia emblem is, among other things, a mark of origin. When it appears on a document, a product, or a page, it says: Meechie's World Inc made this. That function, identifying the maker, is one of the oldest purposes of any emblem. This companion chapter traces the history of makers' marks, signatures, and seals, and shows how the emblem fits into that long tradition of standing behind one's work.

Marks on stone

The earliest makers' marks may be the marks left by stonemasons. Archaeologists have found mason's marks on the stones of ancient buildings across the world, from the pyramids of Egypt to the cathedrals of medieval Europe. In Egypt, as noted in Chapter Eight, work gangs sometimes painted their names on blocks inside the pyramids, with names that boasted of their loyalty to the king. In medieval Europe, individual masons carved small personal symbols into the stones they shaped: a cross, an arrow, a star, a letter, a geometric figure. These marks allowed the master mason to know who had cut each stone, so that workers could be paid for their work and held responsible if a stone was badly cut.

A mason's mark is a small but profound thing. It says: I made this, and I am accountable for it. A worker who carves his mark into a stone is putting his name on his work, knowing that the stone may stand for centuries and that his mark will be seen long after he is gone.

Marks on pots and metal

Potters, too, have marked their work for thousands of years. Ancient Roman potters stamped their names on the bases of their pots and lamps. In the Islamic world, master potters and metalworkers signed their finest pieces. In China, porcelain from the imperial kilns was marked with the reign of the emperor under whom it was made.

The most famous system of makers' marks is the hallmarking of precious metals, which began in medieval Europe. In England, a statute of 1300 required that silver be tested for purity and stamped with a mark, the leopard's head, before it could be sold. The testing took place at the hall of the Goldsmiths' Company in London, which is the origin of the word "hallmark." Over time, hallmarks came to include the maker's mark, the purity mark, the assay office mark, and a date letter showing the year the piece was tested.

A hallmark guarantees two things: that the metal is what it claims to be, and that a known maker stands behind it. The word has passed into everyday language: a "hallmark" of something is its distinguishing sign of quality. The Conscientia emblem is meant to be a hallmark in this sense. Wherever it appears, it should guarantee that the work is genuine and that the house stands behind it.

Seals and signatures

As we saw in Chapters Five and Sixteen, seals were the great instruments of authentication in the ancient and medieval worlds. A seal pressed into wax was the equivalent of a signature, and often more trusted than one, because seals were carefully guarded and difficult to forge.

Signatures as we know them, handwritten names used to authenticate documents, became common in Europe in the later Middle Ages and the early modern period, as literacy spread. In Islamic and Ottoman tradition, rulers used the tughra, an elaborate calligraphic monogram, as a royal signature on decrees and coins. In China, Japan, and Korea, personal and official seals called chops or hanko are still widely used to sign documents.

Today, signatures carry legal weight in most countries. When a person signs a legal document, they affirm that its contents are true, or that they agree to its terms. In American courts, the signature on a filing is a serious matter. Under the federal rules of civil procedure, for example, by signing a paper submitted to the court, a person certifies that, to the best of their knowledge, the legal arguments are warranted and the factual claims have evidentiary support. A false signature can bring penalties.

This is one reason the company's legal documents leave the signature to the client. The client signs, because the client is the one making the claims to the court. The company's emblem at the top of the page is a different kind of mark: not a signature affirming the facts, but a maker's mark showing who prepared the document and guaranteeing the care that went into its preparation.

The signature of a name

Some people use a special form of their name as a signature, a name that carries their identity and their convictions. The founder of Meechie's World Inc uses, as his personal signature, the name Muhammad Abdul Almalik-El, Sovereign, a name in the tradition of Arabic names that reflects his faith and identity. The name Abdul Malik means "servant of the King," the King being God; Muhammad is the name of the Prophet of Islam, the most common name in the Muslim world. A name used as a signature is a statement of who one is, a mark of identity placed at the bottom of one's words.

In this sense, every person has a maker's mark: the name they sign, the way they work, the standard they keep. The emblem of a company is the collective form of the same thing.

Brands and trademarks

The modern descendant of the maker's mark is the brand and the trademark. The word "brand" originally referred to the mark burned onto cattle with a hot iron to show ownership. By the nineteenth century, as factories began producing goods for distant markets, makers used brands and trademarks to distinguish their products from those of competitors and to assure customers of consistent quality. Some of the oldest trademarks still in use date from that period.

Trademark law, as noted in Chapter Seventeen, protects these marks so that customers are not deceived by imitations. The principle behind it is the same as the principle behind the mason's mark and the hallmark: a mark should tell the truth about who made something. A counterfeit mark is a lie.

A mark that must be earned

There is an important difference between having a mark and deserving it. Anyone can design an emblem. Only a maker who does good work can make that emblem mean something. The leopard's head on English silver means "pure silver" only because, for seven centuries, the Goldsmiths' Company has tested silver honestly and refused to mark what fails the test. If the testers had cheated, the mark would mean nothing.

The same is true of the Conscientia emblem. It means "made with conscience" only if every piece of work that carries it is made with conscience. Every honest document adds to its meaning. Every dishonest one would subtract from it. The emblem is not a guarantee in itself. It is a promise that has to be kept, again and again, to stay true.

By their fruits

The Gospel of Matthew, in the verse quoted at the start of this chapter, says that people are known by their fruits. A tree is judged not by its bark or its leaves but by what it produces. A good tree bears good fruit; a bad tree bears bad fruit.

A company is judged the same way. Not by its emblem, however beautiful. Not by its mottos, however noble. Not even by a three-hundred-page book explaining what its symbols mean. It is judged by its work. By the documents it prepares, the songs it records, the websites it builds, the clothes it sells, the families it helps. The emblem is only the label on the fruit.

That is a humbling thought on which to close this book. All the history of the eye, the pyramid, and the book, all the meaning of Conscientia, Lux e tenebris, and Iustitiam quaerimus, comes down in the end to a simple test: is the work good? Is it honest? Does it help?

The mason carved his mark and let the stone speak for him. Meechie's World Inc places its emblem on its work and lets the work speak for it.

Afterword: The Eye in the Mirror

There is an old practice, found in many monasteries and many homes, of keeping a small mirror near the door. Before going out into the world, a person would glance into it, not out of vanity, but as a reminder: this is the face you will show today. Will it be an honest one?

The Conscientia emblem works something like that mirror. Every time it appears at the top of a page, it looks back at the person who made the page. It asks: is this work true? Did you check it? Would you stand behind it if the whole world read it?

In writing this book, we have traveled a long way from that simple question. We have followed the eye through Egypt and Babylon, through the temples of India and the stupas of Nepal, through the churches of Florence and the halls of Congress, through the lodges of the builders and the fevered imaginations of conspiracy theorists. We have climbed the pyramid and studied the triangle. We have opened the book and stood in the light. We have read the word Conscientia and the motto Iustitiam quaerimus. And we have toured the rooms of a young company that has chosen to put all of this on its door.

But in the end, the journey comes back to the mirror. All the history in the world does not make an emblem meaningful. Only the people who carry it can do that. A symbol of conscience carried by dishonest people becomes a lie. A symbol of conscience carried by honest people becomes a light.

The eye in our emblem is not watching you from the sky. It is not a secret society peering through the dollar bill. It is not even, finally, the founder of the company keeping an eye on his business. It is your own eye, looking back at you from the page, asking whether you are living up to what you know.

That is what Conscientia means: the knowledge you share with yourself. The witness you cannot escape. The voice that speaks when no one else is in the room.

May it speak clearly. May you listen. And may the light come out of whatever darkness you are in.

Glossary of Symbols and Terms

Achievement. In heraldry, the complete display of a coat of arms with all its parts: shield, crest, motto, supporters, and other ornaments. The full crest of Meechie's World Inc is its achievement.

All-seeing eye. A general name for an eye used as a symbol of a power that sees everything, especially divine providence or conscience.

Ashlar. A block of cut and dressed stone. In Masonic symbolism, the rough ashlar represents a person in a natural state and the perfect ashlar a person improved by education and virtue.

Benben. A sacred stone at the Egyptian temple of the sun at Heliopolis, representing the first mound of land at creation, associated with the capstones of pyramids and obelisks.

Bookmark. In the Conscientia emblem, the small red ribbon hanging from the open book, marking the reader's place and recalling the red ribbons of legal documents.

Capstone. The top stone of a pyramid. In the Conscientia emblem, the glowing triangle containing the eye, set just above the pyramid.

Codex. A book made of pages bound together along one edge, the form of book used today, which replaced the scroll in late antiquity.

Conscientia. Latin for conscience; literally "knowing with" or "knowing together." The word at the center of the emblem of Meechie's World Inc.

Course. A horizontal layer of stones or bricks in a wall or pyramid. The pyramid of the Conscientia emblem has four courses.

Crest. In everyday use, a distinctive emblem of a family or organization. Meechie's World Inc uses the word for its full circular seal with name, wreath, ribbon, and mottos.

Evil eye. The widespread belief that an envious glance can cause harm, and the protective charms, often themselves shaped like eyes, used to ward it off.

Eye of Horus. The wedjat eye of Egyptian religion, the eye of the falcon god Horus, injured by Set and restored; a symbol of healing, wholeness, and protection.

Eye of Providence. The eye within a triangle, often surrounded by rays, used in Christian art from the Renaissance onward to represent God's watchful care; the eye on the reverse of the Great Seal of the United States.

Eye of Ra. In Egyptian religion, the fierce, often female power of the sun god, identified with goddesses such as Sekhmet and Hathor and with the cobra on the brow of kings.

Field. In heraldry, the background of a shield or emblem. The field of the Conscientia emblem is black.

Glory. In art, a burst of rays surrounding a holy figure or symbol, signifying divine light.

Great Seal of the United States. The official seal of the United States, adopted June 20, 1782. Its obverse shows the bald eagle; its reverse shows the unfinished pyramid with the Eye of Providence.

Laurel. The bay tree, sacred to Apollo; a wreath of its leaves is an ancient symbol of victory, honor, and the arts. The crest of Meechie's World Inc includes a laurel wreath.

Or. The heraldic term for gold.

Pro se. Latin for "for oneself." A pro se litigant is a person who represents himself or herself in court without a lawyer.

Providence. From the Latin for foresight; the belief that God watches over and guides the world.

Pyramidion. The capstone of an Egyptian pyramid or obelisk, sometimes covered in gold or electrum.

Rays. Lines of light radiating from a source. The Conscientia emblem has thirteen rays.

Sable. The heraldic term for black.

Scale. A balance used for weighing; a symbol of justice and of honest dealing. The crest of Meechie's World Inc includes a scale above the motto Iustitiam quaerimus.

Seal. A device for making an impression in wax, clay, or paper to authenticate a document; by extension, the design such a device makes.

Syneidesis. The Greek word for conscience, built like the Latin conscientia from "with" and "knowing."

Third eye. In Hindu and related traditions, an inner eye of spiritual perception, shown on the forehead of the god Shiva.

Triangle. The simplest closed shape made of straight lines and the most rigid in construction; in Christian art a symbol of the Trinity.

Truncated pyramid. A pyramid whose top has been cut off flat. The pyramids on the Great Seal and in the Conscientia emblem are truncated, with the capstone shown separately.

Wedjat. The Egyptian name of the Eye of Horus, meaning "the sound one" or "the whole one."

The Latin of the Emblem

Latin is the language of the emblem's mottos and of many of the traditions behind it. This short guide explains the Latin words and phrases used in the emblem and in this book, with a simple guide to pronunciation in the classical style.

Conscientia (kon-skee-EN-tee-ah). Conscience; knowing together. From con-, "with," and scientia, "knowledge."

Lux e tenebris (LOOKS ay TEN-eh-bris). Light out of darkness. Lux, light; e, out of; tenebris, from tenebrae, darkness. The motto on the golden ribbon of the crest.

Iustitiam quaerimus (yoos-TIT-ee-am KWAI-ri-moos). We seek justice. Iustitiam, justice, as the object of the verb; quaerimus, we seek, we search for. The motto at the base of the crest.

Post tenebras lux (post TEN-eh-brahs LOOKS). After darkness, light. The motto of the city of Geneva, a close relative of Lux e tenebris.

Annuit coeptis (AN-noo-it KOIP-tees). He has favored our undertakings. The motto above the eye on the reverse of the Great Seal.

Novus ordo seclorum (NO-voos OR-doh say-KLOR-oom). A new order of the ages. The motto beneath the pyramid on the reverse of the Great Seal. It does not mean "new world order."

E pluribus unum (ay PLOO-ri-boos OO-noom). Out of many, one. The motto on the obverse of the Great Seal.

MDCCLXXVI. The year 1776 in Roman numerals, on the base of the pyramid on the Great Seal.

Perennis (peh-REN-nis). Everlasting, enduring. A motto used with the unfinished pyramid on early American currency.

Deo favente (DAY-oh fah-WEN-tay). With God favoring. A motto proposed by William Barton for the Great Seal.

Providentia (pro-wee-DEN-tee-ah). Foresight; providence. From pro, ahead, and videre, to see.

Iustitia est constans et perpetua voluntas ius suum cuique tribuendi. Justice is the constant and perpetual will to render to each person what is due. The definition of justice by the Roman jurist Ulpian.

Pro se (proh say). For oneself. Used of a person who represents himself or herself in court.

Integer (IN-teh-ger). Whole, undivided. The root of the English word integrity.

A Timeline of the Eye

Dates in the ancient world are approximate.

c. 3500 to 3300 BCE. Eye idols are made at Tell Brak in northern Syria.

c. 3300 to 3200 BCE. Writing begins in Mesopotamia, first used largely for keeping records.

c. 3100 BCE. Egypt is unified; Egyptian civilization begins its long history.

c. 2650 BCE. Imhotep builds the Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara.

c. 2560 BCE. The Great Pyramid of Khufu is built at Giza.

c. 1850 to 1815 BCE. The pyramidion of Amenemhat III, carved with wedjat eyes, is made in Egypt's Middle Kingdom.

c. 1750 BCE. The laws of Hammurabi are carved beneath an image of the all-seeing sun god Shamash.

6th century BCE. Greek eye cups are painted with large protective eyes.

c. 300 BCE. Euclid writes the Elements in Alexandria, beginning with the construction of the equilateral triangle.

1st century BCE. Cicero writes of conscience as more important than the opinion of the world.

1st century CE. The apostle Paul writes of conscience bearing witness in human hearts.

6th century. The Digest of Justinian opens with Ulpian's definition of justice.

c. 1000. Ibn al-Haytham, in Cairo, writes the Book of Optics, explaining vision as light entering the eye.

13th century. Thomas Aquinas distinguishes synderesis and conscientia.

c. 1450. Gutenberg's printing press makes books widely available in Europe.

1494. Sebastian Brant's Ship of Fools shows a blindfolded Justice.

1525. Pontormo paints the Supper at Emmaus with an eye in a triangle above Christ.

1531. Alciato's Emblemata begins the fashion for emblem books.

1717. The first Grand Lodge of Freemasons is formed in London.

1775. Prince Hall and fourteen other free Black men are initiated into Freemasonry in Boston.

1776, May 1. Adam Weishaupt founds the Bavarian Illuminati.

1776, July 4. Congress adopts the Declaration of Independence and appoints the first committee to design a seal; du Simitière proposes the Eye of Providence.

1778. Francis Hopkinson's fifty-dollar Continental note shows an unfinished pyramid with the word Perennis.

1782, June 20. Congress adopts the Great Seal of the United States, with the eye above the unfinished pyramid on its reverse.

1784 to 1785. The Bavarian government bans secret societies, ending the Illuminati.

1784 to 1787. African Lodge No. 459 receives its warrant from the Grand Lodge of England.

1797. Thomas Smith Webb's Freemason's Monitor describes the All-Seeing Eye; Barruel and Robison publish conspiracy theories about the Illuminati.

1819. Jeremy Cross's True Masonic Chart spreads the Masonic eye in illustrations.

1826 to 1831. The William Morgan affair leads to the Anti-Masonic Party.

1935. The reverse of the Great Seal appears on the one-dollar bill.

1975. The satirical Illuminatus! trilogy is published.

2013. The founder of Meechie's World Inc begins building an online catalog of his music.

2026, October. Meechie's World Inc is formally organized; its website opens; the Conscientia emblem and crest become the marks of the house; this book is written.

Further Reading

The following are good places to learn more about the subjects of this book. They range from scholarly works to accessible introductions and official sources.

On the Great Seal. Richard S. Patterson and Richardson Dougall, The Eagle and the Shield: A History of the Great Seal of the United States, published by the U.S. Department of State, 1976. The standard history, with the full record of the committees and Charles Thomson's report. The U.S. Department of State and the Bureau of Engraving and Printing also publish short official histories of the seal and of the one-dollar bill.

On Egyptian symbols. Richard H. Wilkinson, Reading Egyptian Art: A Hieroglyphic Guide to Ancient Egyptian Painting and Sculpture, and The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt. Clear, well-illustrated guides to the Eye of Horus, the Eye of Ra, and the symbolism of the pyramids.

On the pyramids and their builders. Mark Lehner, The Complete Pyramids. A comprehensive survey by an archaeologist who led excavations of the pyramid builders' settlement at Giza.

On Christian symbolism. George Ferguson, Signs and Symbols in Christian Art. A classic, accessible guide to the meanings of symbols such as the Eye of Providence, the triangle, and the glory.

On Freemasonry. Margaret C. Jacob, The Origins of Freemasonry: Facts and Fictions. A historian's account of the movement's beginnings. On Prince Hall Freemasonry, the work of historians such as Corey D. B. Walker and the publications of the Prince Hall Grand Lodges provide a rich record.

On the Illuminati and conspiracy theories. Many historians have written on the Bavarian Illuminati and the growth of conspiracy theories after the French Revolution; general histories of the Enlightenment and of the 1790s cover the subject well. Reputable encyclopedias offer reliable short overviews.

On conscience. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae, the questions on synderesis and conscience. Martin Luther King Jr., Letter from Birmingham Jail. Both remain among the most powerful writings on conscience and justice.

On Latin. Any good Latin dictionary, such as the Oxford Latin Dictionary or Lewis and Short, will show the full range of meaning of conscientia, iustitia, and quaerere.

On representing yourself in court. Many courts publish free guides and forms for self-represented litigants, and many states have court self-help centers and legal aid organizations. The website of your local court is the best starting point. This book does not give legal advice; anyone facing a legal matter should consult a licensed attorney where possible.

On heraldry. Stephen Friar, editor, A New Dictionary of Heraldry, and general introductions to heraldry published by heraldic societies, explain terms such as achievement, field, or, and sable.
